sayThis.en: "Your desk is your shop. Sign on the front with your name. Then a card for every single thing you brought — what it is, what shape it's in, and what you'd want in return. Nobody trades for something they can't read about first."
sayThis.es: "Your desk is your shop. Sign on the front with your name. Then a card for every single thing you brought — what it is, what shape it's in, and what you'd want in return. Nobody trades for something they can't read about first."

doneWhen.en: Every desk has a name sign and a card sitting beside every item.
doneWhen.es: Every desk has a name sign and a card sitting beside every item.

watchFor.en: One-word cards. "Good." Ask them whether they'd trade for that card.
watchFor.es: One-word cards. "Good." Ask them whether they'd trade for that card.

description.en: Create booth sign with student name: "[Name]'s Swap Station" - For each item: detailed value card including why it's valuable, condition, what you'd trade it for - Optional: create small advertisement poster for your most valuable item.
description.es: Create booth sign with student name: "[Name]'s Swap Station" - For each item: detailed value card including why it's valuable, condition, what you'd trade it for - Optional: create small advertisement poster for your most valuable item.

description.en: Each child makes a sign with their name on it. Then they draw their item on a card with crayons and say out loud what they would trade it for.
description.es: Each child makes a sign with their name on it. Then they draw their item on a card with crayons and say out loud what they would trade it for.

sayThis.en: "Your desk is your shop. Put your name on your sign. Draw your thing on a card. Then tell a friend what you would trade it for."
sayThis.es: "Your desk is your shop. Put your name on your sign. Draw your thing on a card. Then tell a friend what you would trade it for."

watchFor.en: Kids who can't write their name yet. Write it lightly with a pencil and let them trace it with a crayon.
watchFor.es: Kids who can't write their name yet. Write it lightly with a pencil and let them trace it with a crayon.

doneWhen.en: Every desk has a name sign and a card with a drawing beside the item.
doneWhen.es: Every desk has a name sign and a card with a drawing beside the item.

sayThis.en: "Three things you're allowed to say. 'I'll trade this for that' — that's an offer. 'Only if you add something' — that's a counter. Then you either shake hands, or you say no thank you and walk away. Walking away is a legal move. It is not rude."
sayThis.es: "Three things you're allowed to say. 'I'll trade this for that' — that's an offer. 'Only if you add something' — that's a counter. Then you either shake hands, or you say no thank you and walk away. Walking away is a legal move. It is not rude."

doneWhen.en: Two volunteers have acted out an offer, a counter and a no-deal in front of the class.
doneWhen.es: Two volunteers have acted out an offer, a counter and a no-deal in front of the class.

watchFor.en: Students who think every offer has to be accepted. Say the walk-away rule out loud before anyone trades.
watchFor.es: Students who think every offer has to be accepted. Say the walk-away rule out loud before anyone trades.

description.en: Teacher models: "Opening offer" ("I'll trade this book for that toy") - "Counter-offer" ("I'll only trade if you add something else") - "Agreement" (both shake hands) or "No deal" (polite decline)
description.es: Teacher models: "Opening offer" ("I'll trade this book for that toy") - "Counter-offer" ("I'll only trade if you add something else") - "Agreement" (both shake hands) or "No deal" (polite decline)

sayThis.en: "Sellers stay at your desk. Shoppers, eight minutes. You do not have to trade at all. Read the card before you ask."
sayThis.es: "Sellers stay at your desk. Shoppers, eight minutes. You do not have to trade at all. Read the card before you ask."

doneWhen.en: Every seller is at their desk and every shopper has visited at least three booths.
doneWhen.es: Every seller is at their desk and every shopper has visited at least three booths.

watchFor.en: The loud trader clearing the room in two minutes, and the quiet booth nobody visits. Walk a shopper over yourself.
watchFor.es: The loud trader clearing the room in two minutes, and the quiet booth nobody visits. Walk a shopper over yourself.

description.en: Half class shops, half minds booths. Negotiation and trading.
description.es: Half class shops, half minds booths. Negotiation and trading.

sayThis.en: "Swap over. Shoppers are sellers now. If your things changed hands, sell whatever you ended up with. Same three moves."
sayThis.es: "Swap over. Shoppers are sellers now. If your things changed hands, sell whatever you ended up with. Same three moves."

doneWhen.en: Every student has been on both sides and every booth is staffed.
doneWhen.es: Every student has been on both sides and every booth is staffed.

watchFor.en: Students who refuse to re-trade something they just got. That's a fine answer. Say so out loud so nobody pushes them.
watchFor.es: Students who refuse to re-trade something they just got. That's a fine answer. Say so out loud so nobody pushes them.

description.en: Shoppers become sellers, sellers become shoppers.
description.es: Shoppers become sellers, sellers become shoppers.

sayThis.en: "Four boxes. What you brought. What you gave away. What you're holding now. And a number out of ten for how you feel about it. Then every ten goes on the board."
sayThis.es: "Four boxes. What you brought. What you gave away. What you're holding now. And a number out of ten for how you feel about it. Then every ten goes on the board."

doneWhen.en: Every tracking sheet has all four boxes filled and the class trade count is on the board.

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Teach the trade with gestures first: point to your item, point to theirs, ask "Trade?" Nod for yes, hand up for no thank you.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Post the trade steps as pictures: show your item, ask to trade, yes or no thank you, swap.

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Teach buy, sell, price, cheap and expensive with the coins and cup cards in hand.
Give sellers one sentence to say: "One cup is ___ coins." Customers can point and hold out the coins.
Put pictures on the board tally: a cup for cups sold, a coin for money taken in.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Give each customer their ten coins in a small pile or ten-frame so they can see what is left.
Let a student be the stand's cup-hander or tally-keeper instead of calling out to customers.
Pre-write the price sign for a student who struggles with writing.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Work out each stand's money as cups sold times price, and check it against the coin count.
Predict before round two which price will take in the most coins, then check.
Make a bar graph of round one and round two for every stand.

Let students count their bookmarks in their home language first, then in English.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Give a student one clear job with a picture card at the station, such as "You only fold."
Pair a student who finds cutting or tearing hard with a partner in the solo round, or prepare their paper for them.
Offer a quieter station at the end of the line if the room gets noisy.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Time each station and find the slowest job, then suggest how to fix it.
Work out bookmarks per person for the team and for solo, and say which is faster.
Redesign the line for a third round: move people to the slow job and predict the new total.

Sentence frames: "This is ___. It comes from ___. It's special because ___."
Basic map work (marking where an item comes from)
Vocabulary: heritage, culture, tradition, value, travel
Written descriptions with some detail
Independent map work (finding countries)
Understanding how items travel to a family
Vocabulary: origin, inherited, souvenir, cultural value, heirloom
Detailed written descriptions and stories
Present an item and answer questions about it
Understanding global connections shown on the map
Advanced vocabulary: origin, cultural heritage, ancestral, provenance, priceless

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Let students label their drawings in their home language, with English beside it if they can.
Give the frame: "This is ___. It comes from ___. It's special because ___."
Find the place on the world map together before the student has to say its name.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Let a student draw items instead of writing, and write one sentence for them as they tell you.
Lower the count to two or three items.
Offer the prompt cards (a food, a holiday, a place, a person) to a student who gets stuck choosing.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Find each item's country on the map and work out roughly how far it traveled to get here.
Add a store price and a family value to each card, and explain why they are different.
Interview a family member and write the story of how one item came to the family.

description.en: Show the spice clue cards. Discuss: What are spices? Where do they come from? How do people use them? Explain the smell-clue game: listen to the clue, remember the smell, guess the spice.
description.es: Show the spice clue cards. Discuss: What are spices? Where do they come from? How do people use them? Explain the smell-clue game: listen to the clue, remember the smell, guess the spice.

sayThis.en: "Spices are dried plant parts that make food smell and taste good. Long ago, people sailed across the world to get them. Today you're detectives. I read a smell clue. You remember that smell and guess the spice."
sayThis.es: "Spices are dried plant parts that make food smell and taste good. Long ago, people sailed across the world to get them. Today you're detectives. I read a smell clue. You remember that smell and guess the spice."

watchFor.en: Kids who say they have never smelled a spice. Ask about toothpaste, gingerbread or pizza. They have.
watchFor.es: Kids who say they have never smelled a spice. Ask about toothpaste, gingerbread or pizza. They have.

doneWhen.en: Every child can say the game: listen to the clue, remember the smell, guess.
doneWhen.es: Every child can say the game: listen to the clue, remember the smell, guess.

description.en: Skip where spices come from and the sailing history. Say in one line what a spice is, then teach the game: I read a clue, you think of the smell, you guess.
description.es: Skip where spices come from and the sailing history. Say in one line what a spice is, then teach the game: I read a clue, you think of the smell, you guess.

sayThis.en: "Spices are dried bits of plants that make food smell good. Today you are smell detectives. I read a clue. You think of that smell. Then you guess the spice."
sayThis.es: "Spices are dried bits of plants that make food smell good. Today you are smell detectives. I read a clue. You think of that smell. Then you guess the spice."

doneWhen.en: Every child has a blank card and a crayon in front of them and the class has said "listen, remember, guess" together.
doneWhen.es: Every child has a blank card and a crayon in front of them and the class has said "listen, remember, guess" together.

description.en: Read the smell clue on each card (cinnamon, pepper, mint, ginger, cloves). Students remember the smell and try to identify each spice. Notice: sweet, spicy, strong, mild. Record each guess with a crayon drawing or words on a small card.
description.es: Read the smell clue on each card (cinnamon, pepper, mint, ginger, cloves). Students remember the smell and try to identify each spice. Notice: sweet, spicy, strong, mild. Record each guess with a crayon drawing or words on a small card.

sayThis.en: "Close your eyes. Listen to the clue. Can you remember that smell? Is it sweet? Spicy? Strong? Draw your guess on a card."
sayThis.es: "Close your eyes. Listen to the clue. Can you remember that smell? Is it sweet? Spicy? Strong? Draw your guess on a card."

watchFor.en: Kids who can't remember a smell. Name a food it is in: cinnamon toast, pepper on pizza, mint toothpaste.
watchFor.es: Kids who can't remember a smell. Name a food it is in: cinnamon toast, pepper on pizza, mint toothpaste.

doneWhen.en: Every child has a card for each clue, and you have turned the clue cards over to show the real names.
doneWhen.es: Every child has a card for each clue, and you have turned the clue cards over to show the real names.

description.en: Use three clue cards only: cinnamon, mint and pepper. Children draw their guess. No writing. Give them the smell words out loud: sweet, spicy, strong.
description.es: Use three clue cards only: cinnamon, mint and pepper. Children draw their guess. No writing. Give them the smell words out loud: sweet, spicy, strong.

sayThis.en: "Close your eyes. Listen to my clue. Can you smell it in your head? Is it sweet or is it spicy? Now draw your guess."
sayThis.es: "Close your eyes. Listen to my clue. Can you smell it in your head? Is it sweet or is it spicy? Now draw your guess."

doneWhen.en: Every child has three cards with a drawing on each, and the real names are showing on the clue cards.
doneWhen.es: Every child has three cards with a drawing on each, and the real names are showing on the clue cards.

description.en: Sort the spice cards into categories students choose: by smell (strong/mild), by use (cooking/baking), by color, or by preference (like/don't like). Draw the sorting chart on the board.
description.es: Sort the spice cards into categories students choose: by smell (strong/mild), by use (cooking/baking), by color, or by preference (like/don't like). Draw the sorting chart on the board.

sayThis.en: "Put your cards in two piles. Strong smells here, soft smells there. Or: ones you like, ones you don't."
sayThis.es: "Put your cards in two piles. Strong smells here, soft smells there. Or: ones you like, ones you don't."

watchFor.en: Kids who can't decide. Ask, "Does it make you sneeze?" If yes, it's strong.
watchFor.es: Kids who can't decide. Ask, "Does it make you sneeze?" If yes, it's strong.

doneWhen.en: The chart on the board shows every spice in a group.
doneWhen.es: The chart on the board shows every spice in a group.

description.en: One sort only: spices I like and spices I do not like. Draw two big circles on the board and let the children put their cards in. Skip the other ways to sort.
description.es: One sort only: spices I like and spices I do not like. Draw two big circles on the board and let the children put their cards in. Skip the other ways to sort.

sayThis.en: "Two piles. Ones you like go here. Ones you do not like go there. Put every card in one pile or the other."
sayThis.es: "Two piles. Ones you like go here. Ones you do not like go there. Put every card in one pile or the other."

watchFor.en: Kids who cannot decide. Ask if they would eat it on toast. Yes goes in the like pile.
watchFor.es: Kids who cannot decide. Ask if they would eat it on toast. Yes goes in the like pile.

doneWhen.en: Every card is in one of the two circles and no cards are left in anyone's hands.
doneWhen.es: Every card is in one of the two circles and no cards are left in anyone's hands.

description.en: Pretend spices are valuable trade goods. Students 'trade' spice cards with partners. Discuss: Why were spices valuable in history? Why did people trade them across long distances?
description.es: Pretend spices are valuable trade goods. Students 'trade' spice cards with partners. Discuss: Why were spices valuable in history? Why did people trade them across long distances?

sayThis.en: "Long ago, spices were like treasure. Your cards are treasure now. Find a partner and trade one card for one card."
sayThis.es: "Long ago, spices were like treasure. Your cards are treasure now. Find a partner and trade one card for one card."

watchFor.en: Kids who won't give up their favorite card. That's fine. Remind them they can say no thank you.
watchFor.es: Kids who won't give up their favorite card. That's fine. Remind them they can say no thank you.

doneWhen.en: Every child has made one trade or said no thank you.
doneWhen.es: Every child has made one trade or said no thank you.

description.en: One trade each, one card for one card. Say spices used to be treasure and stop there. Skip the questions about why people traded them so far.
description.es: One trade each, one card for one card. Say spices used to be treasure and stop there. Skip the questions about why people traded them so far.

description.en: Discuss: What surprised you about spices? Which was your favorite smell? How do spices add value to food? Where do spices in our kitchen come from?
description.es: Discuss: What surprised you about spices? Which was your favorite smell? How do spices add value to food? Where do spices in our kitchen come from?

sayThis.en: "Which smell was your favorite? Which one surprised you?"
sayThis.es: "Which smell was your favorite? Which one surprised you?"

watchFor.en: Nothing much in two minutes. Take two or three answers and stop.
watchFor.es: Nothing much in two minutes. Take two or three answers and stop.

doneWhen.en: Three children have named a favorite smell.
doneWhen.es: Three children have named a favorite smell.

description.en: One question only: which smell was your favorite? Skip the question about where kitchen spices come from.
description.es: One question only: which smell was your favorite? Skip the question about where kitchen spices come from.

sayThis.en: "Which smell was your favorite? Point to that card."
sayThis.es: "Which smell was your favorite? Point to that card."

watchFor.en: A long silence. Name your own favorite first, then take two answers and stop.
watchFor.es: A long silence. Name your own favorite first, then take two answers and stop.

doneWhen.en: Three children have pointed at a card and named the smell.
doneWhen.es: Three children have pointed at a card and named the smell.

discussionQuestions: Which spice smelled best to you?
If everyone wants cinnamon but there's only a little, what happens to its price?
Where do spices come from?

beforeClass.en: Make five spice clue cards on scrap paper, numbered 1 to 5. On the front, write a smell clue: cinnamon smells sweet and warm, like apple pie; black pepper is sharp and makes you sneeze; mint is cool, like toothpaste; ginger is hot and fresh, like gingerbread; cloves are strong and sweet. On the back, write the name and draw the spice with a crayon. Tear scrap paper into small cards, five per student; kids draw one spice per card as they guess, and trade those cards later.
beforeClass.es: Make five spice clue cards on scrap paper, numbered 1 to 5. On the front, write a smell clue: cinnamon smells sweet and warm, like apple pie; black pepper is sharp and makes you sneeze; mint is cool, like toothpaste; ginger is hot and fresh, like gingerbread; cloves are strong and sweet. On the back, write the name and draw the spice with a crayon. Tear scrap paper into small cards, five per student; kids draw one spice per card as they guess, and trade those cards later.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: sort one way only in the Spice Sorting Activity, strong or mild. Short: add a second sort in the Spice Sorting Activity, by color.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: sort one way only in the Spice Sorting Activity, strong or mild. Short: add a second sort in the Spice Sorting Activity, by color.

description.en: Introduce spices from around the world. Discuss trade routes, how spices traveled, why they were valuable. Explain detective activity: hear smell clues, identify, sort, and trade spice cards.
description.es: Introduce spices from around the world. Discuss trade routes, how spices traveled, why they were valuable. Explain detective activity: hear smell clues, identify, sort, and trade spice cards.

sayThis.en: "Long ago, spices were so valuable that people sailed for months to get them. Today you're spice detectives. You'll hear smell clues, name the spices, sort them and trade them."
sayThis.es: "Long ago, spices were so valuable that people sailed for months to get them. Today you're spice detectives. You'll hear smell clues, name the spices, sort them and trade them."

watchFor.en: Kids flipping the clue cards to peek at the names. Keep the cards face down until the next step starts.
watchFor.es: Kids flipping the clue cards to peek at the names. Keep the cards face down until the next step starts.

doneWhen.en: Every student can say the four jobs: listen, name, sort, trade.
doneWhen.es: Every student can say the four jobs: listen, name, sort, trade.

description.en: Read each spice clue aloud: its smell, its color and how it looks. Students record with a pencil on observation sheets: smell description, color, look, and a guess of what it is. Compare guesses with the real spice names on the back of the cards.
description.es: Read each spice clue aloud: its smell, its color and how it looks. Students record with a pencil on observation sheets: smell description, color, look, and a guess of what it is. Compare guesses with the real spice names on the back of the cards.

sayThis.en: "Listen to the clue and remember that smell. Write what it smells like, what color it is and how it looks. Then guess its name."
sayThis.es: "Listen to the clue and remember that smell. Write what it smells like, what color it is and how it looks. Then guess its name."

watchFor.en: "I don't know that smell." Name a food it is in, like cinnamon toast or pepper on pizza.
watchFor.es: "I don't know that smell." Name a food it is in, like cinnamon toast or pepper on pizza.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has a guess for every clue card, and you have read out the real names.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has a guess for every clue card, and you have read out the real names.

description.en: Read each smell clue aloud. Children draw each spice with crayons and say one smell word: sweet, spicy, strong or mild. Turn the clue card over and read the real name together.
description.es: Read each smell clue aloud. Children draw each spice with crayons and say one smell word: sweet, spicy, strong or mild. Turn the clue card over and read the real name together.

sayThis.en: "Listen to the clue. What does it smell like? Say one word. Now draw it."
sayThis.es: "Listen to the clue. What does it smell like? Say one word. Now draw it."

watchFor.en: Children who cannot think of a word. Give two to choose from: sweet or spicy?
watchFor.es: Children who cannot think of a word. Give two to choose from: sweet or spicy?

doneWhen.en: Every child has a drawing for every clue card and has said one smell word.
doneWhen.es: Every child has a drawing for every clue card and has said one smell word.

description.en: Sort spices multiple ways: by origin (where they come from), by use (cooking vs baking), by intensity (mild to strong), by preference. Create detailed sorting charts or graphs on scrap paper.
description.es: Sort spices multiple ways: by origin (where they come from), by use (cooking vs baking), by intensity (mild to strong), by preference. Create detailed sorting charts or graphs on scrap paper.

sayThis.en: "Sort the spices one way. Now sort them a different way. Where do they come from? Cooking or baking? Mild or strong? Make a chart."
sayThis.es: "Sort the spices one way. Now sort them a different way. Where do they come from? Cooking or baking? Mild or strong? Make a chart."

watchFor.en: Groups sorting once and stopping. Ask for a second way to sort the same spices.
watchFor.es: Groups sorting once and stopping. Ask for a second way to sort the same spices.

doneWhen.en: Every group has a chart with every spice on it.
doneWhen.es: Every group has a chart with every spice on it.

description.en: Sort the spice cards two ways: like or don't like, then strong or mild. Draw the piles on scrap paper with crayons.
description.es: Sort the spice cards two ways: like or don't like, then strong or mild. Draw the piles on scrap paper with crayons.

sayThis.en: "Put the spices you like here and the ones you don't like there. Now mix them up. Strong smells here, mild smells there."
sayThis.es: "Put the spices you like here and the ones you don't like there. Now mix them up. Strong smells here, mild smells there."

watchFor.en: Children who cannot decide. Ask: did the clue say it makes you sneeze? Then it is strong.
watchFor.es: Children who cannot decide. Ask: did the clue say it makes you sneeze? Then it is strong.

doneWhen.en: Every group has sorted two ways and drawn its piles.
doneWhen.es: Every group has sorted two ways and drawn its piles.

description.en: Simulate spice trade: students receive spice cards and 'trade' to collect full sets. Discuss why certain spices were worth more. Learn about historical spice routes and economics of scarcity.
description.es: Simulate spice trade: students receive spice cards and 'trade' to collect full sets. Discuss why certain spices were worth more. Learn about historical spice routes and economics of scarcity.

sayThis.en: "You each have three spice cards. Trade to collect a full set. One spice is rare. Watch what happens to that card."
sayThis.es: "You each have three spice cards. Trade to collect a full set. One spice is rare. Watch what happens to that card."

watchFor.en: Kids giving away the rare card for one common card. Ask, "How many of those are in the room?"
watchFor.es: Kids giving away the rare card for one common card. Ask, "How many of those are in the room?"

doneWhen.en: Every student has traded at least once, and the class knows which card was hardest to get.
doneWhen.es: Every student has traded at least once, and the class knows which card was hardest to get.

description.en: Each child has three spice cards. Trade one card for one card with a partner. One spice has only a few cards. Notice which card is hard to get.
description.es: Each child has three spice cards. Trade one card for one card with a partner. One spice has only a few cards. Notice which card is hard to get.

sayThis.en: "Trade one card for one card. Look: there are only a few of one card. Which one is it?"
sayThis.es: "Trade one card for one card. Look: there are only a few of one card. Which one is it?"

watchFor.en: Kids giving away the rare card fast. Ask, "How many of those are in the room?"
watchFor.es: Kids giving away the rare card fast. Ask, "How many of those are in the room?"

doneWhen.en: Every child has traded once, and the class knows which card was hardest to get.
doneWhen.es: Every child has traded once, and the class knows which card was hardest to get.

description.en: Reflect on activity: What makes spices valuable? How does smell affect value? Why do people pay more for certain spices? Connect to modern grocery store prices. Discuss cultural importance of spices.
description.es: Reflect on activity: What makes spices valuable? How does smell affect value? Why do people pay more for certain spices? Connect to modern grocery store prices. Discuss cultural importance of spices.

sayThis.en: "Which spice was hardest to get? Why did people long ago pay so much for spices? Which spices does your family cook with?"
sayThis.es: "Which spice was hardest to get? Why did people long ago pay so much for spices? Which spices does your family cook with?"

watchFor.en: Kids saying the best-smelling spice is worth the most. Ask whether it was also the rarest.
watchFor.es: Kids saying the best-smelling spice is worth the most. Ask whether it was also the rarest.

doneWhen.en: One reason spices were valuable is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: One reason spices were valuable is written on the board.

discussionQuestions: Which spices were easiest to trade for? Why?
Which were hardest? Why?
How does rarity affect value?
How did you decide what to trade?

beforeClass.en: Make six to eight numbered spice clue cards on scrap paper. On the front, write a smell clue plus the color and look (cinnamon: sweet and warm, brown curled bark). On the back, write the name and draw the spice with a crayon. Make scrap-paper observation sheets with columns for smell, color, look and guess, and tear small spice cards, three per student, with fewer cards for one spice so it is rare.
beforeClass.es: Make six to eight numbered spice clue cards on scrap paper. On the front, write a smell clue plus the color and look (cinnamon: sweet and warm, brown curled bark). On the back, write the name and draw the spice with a crayon. Make scrap-paper observation sheets with columns for smell, color, look and guess, and tear small spice cards, three per student, with fewer cards for one spice so it is rare.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: sort only two ways in Spice Sorting & Classification, and cut the Spice Market Discussion to two questions. Short: run a second round of the Historical Trade Simulation and see if the rare card gets harder to get.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: sort only two ways in Spice Sorting & Classification, and cut the Spice Market Discussion to two questions. Short: run a second round of the Historical Trade Simulation and see if the rare card gets harder to get.

sayThis.en: "There was a time when a sack of pepper was worth more than the same weight in silver. People sailed for years to get it. Today it's three dollars at the shop. Today you work out what changed."
sayThis.es: "There was a time when a sack of pepper was worth more than the same weight in silver. People sailed for years to get it. Today it's three dollars at the shop. Today you work out what changed."

doneWhen.en: The spice routes are shown on the world map and one reason spices were valuable is written on the board.
doneWhen.es: The spice routes are shown on the world map and one reason spices were valuable is written on the board.

watchFor.en: Flat disbelief that a spice could be money. Stay with it. That disbelief is the hook.
watchFor.es: Flat disbelief that a spice could be money. Stay with it. That disbelief is the hook.

description.en: Discuss historical spice trade: ancient routes, why spices were valuable as gold, cultural significance across civilizations. Show the spice routes on the world map. Explain extended spice detective investigation.
description.es: Discuss historical spice trade: ancient routes, why spices were valuable as gold, cultural significance across civilizations. Show the spice routes on the world map. Explain extended spice detective investigation.

sayThis.en: "Read the clue card. Three words for each one: the color, the smell, and what it reminds you of."
sayThis.es: "Read the clue card. Three words for each one: the color, the smell, and what it reminds you of."

doneWhen.en: Every observation sheet has three words for every station.
doneWhen.es: Every observation sheet has three words for every station.

watchFor.en: Groups copying the clue word for word. Ask what that smell reminds them of at home. Also the student who says every spice sounds the same — read cinnamon and pepper back to back.
watchFor.es: Groups copying the clue word for word. Ask what that smell reminds them of at home. Also the student who says every spice sounds the same — read cinnamon and pepper back to back.

description.en: Students rotate through spice stations: read the clue card, look at the drawing for color and shape, describe the smell in words, record detailed observations with a pencil. Use scientific observation sheets.
description.es: Students rotate through spice stations: read the clue card, look at the drawing for color and shape, describe the smell in words, record detailed observations with a pencil. Use scientific observation sheets.

description.en: Groups visit each station. Read the clue card together, look at the drawing, and say one smell word. Children draw each spice with crayons on their sheet.
description.es: Groups visit each station. Read the clue card together, look at the drawing, and say one smell word. Children draw each spice with crayons on their sheet.

sayThis.en: "Look at the picture. Listen to the clue. Say one smell word: sweet, spicy, strong or mild. Now draw it."
sayThis.es: "Look at the picture. Listen to the clue. Say one smell word: sweet, spicy, strong or mild. Now draw it."

watchFor.en: Children who cannot read the clue. A partner or the teacher reads it aloud.
watchFor.es: Children who cannot read the clue. A partner or the teacher reads it aloud.

doneWhen.en: Every child has a drawing and one smell word for every station.
doneWhen.es: Every child has a drawing and one smell word for every station.

sayThis.en: "Sort them. Any way you like, but you have to defend it. Strong and mild. Sweet and sharp. Near and far. Cheap and dear. Then draw it so we can see your thinking."
sayThis.es: "Sort them. Any way you like, but you have to defend it. Strong and mild. Sweet and sharp. Near and far. Cheap and dear. Then draw it so we can see your thinking."

doneWhen.en: Every group's chart is drawn with every spice placed on it.
doneWhen.es: Every group's chart is drawn with every spice placed on it.

watchFor.en: Groups sorting one way and stopping. Ask for a second way of sorting the same cards.
watchFor.es: Groups sorting one way and stopping. Ask for a second way of sorting the same cards.

description.en: Students create complex classification systems: organize spice cards by multiple characteristics (origin, use, intensity, price, cultural significance). Create Venn diagrams or multi-category charts on scrap paper. Use the world map to find where spices come from.
description.es: Students create complex classification systems: organize spice cards by multiple characteristics (origin, use, intensity, price, cultural significance). Create Venn diagrams or multi-category charts on scrap paper. Use the world map to find where spices come from.

description.en: Sort the spice cards into two piles, like and don't like, and draw the two piles with crayons.
description.es: Sort the spice cards into two piles, like and don't like, and draw the two piles with crayons.

sayThis.en: "Put the spices you like here and the ones you don't like there. Now draw your two piles."
sayThis.es: "Put the spices you like here and the ones you don't like there. Now draw your two piles."

watchFor.en: Children who like them all. Ask: which one would you leave out?
watchFor.es: Children who like them all. Ask: which one would you leave out?

doneWhen.en: Every group has drawn two piles with every spice in one.
doneWhen.es: Every group has drawn two piles with every spice in one.

sayThis.en: "You're a merchant. Some of you are holding something everybody wants and nobody else has. Some of you have what everyone already has. Fill your order — and watch what your rare one is worth by the end."
sayThis.es: "You're a merchant. Some of you are holding something everybody wants and nobody else has. Some of you have what everyone already has. Fill your order — and watch what your rare one is worth by the end."

doneWhen.en: Every merchant's order sheet shows what they traded away and what they got back.
doneWhen.es: Every merchant's order sheet shows what they traded away and what they got back.

watchFor.en: Rare-spice holders trading them away at the same rate as common ones. Ask what something is worth when there's only one of it.
watchFor.es: Rare-spice holders trading them away at the same rate as common ones. Ask what something is worth when there's only one of it.

description.en: Extended trading simulation: students are merchants with different spice cards. Some spices are rare (high value), some common (low value). Trade to complete orders. Track profit. Discuss supply, demand, and scarcity.
description.es: Extended trading simulation: students are merchants with different spice cards. Some spices are rare (high value), some common (low value). Trade to complete orders. Track profit. Discuss supply, demand, and scarcity.

description.en: Children are merchants with spice cards. Some spices have only a few cards (rare). Some have lots (common). Trade one card for one card to fill your order sheet. Talk about it: which cards were hard to get?
description.es: Children are merchants with spice cards. Some spices have only a few cards (rare). Some have lots (common). Trade one card for one card to fill your order sheet. Talk about it: which cards were hard to get?

sayThis.en: "You're a merchant. Look at your order sheet. Trade one card for one card to fill it. Watch the rare card. Does anyone want to give it away?"
sayThis.es: "You're a merchant. Look at your order sheet. Trade one card for one card to fill it. Watch the rare card. Does anyone want to give it away?"

watchFor.en: Kids trading the rare card for any common one. Ask, "How many of those are in the room?"
watchFor.es: Kids trading the rare card for any common one. Ask, "How many of those are in the room?"

doneWhen.en: Every merchant's order sheet shows what they traded away and what they got back.
doneWhen.es: Every merchant's order sheet shows what they traded away and what they got back.

sayThis.en: "Pick a country. Find one spice that country cooks with nearly every day. Two facts and one dish. Then tell us."
sayThis.es: "Pick a country. Find one spice that country cooks with nearly every day. Two facts and one dish. Then tell us."

doneWhen.en: Every pair has reported a country, a spice and a dish.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has reported a country, a spice and a dish.

watchFor.en: Pairs telling a long story. Two facts and one dish. Hold them to it.
watchFor.es: Pairs telling a long story. Two facts and one dish. Hold them to it.

description.en: In pairs, students research how different cultures use specific spices: Indian curry, Mexican chili, Italian basil, Chinese five-spice. Pairs use the world map, the clue cards and what they know about food at home. Present findings. Discuss how spices connect to cultural identity.
description.es: In pairs, students research how different cultures use specific spices: Indian curry, Mexican chili, Italian basil, Chinese five-spice. Pairs use the world map, the clue cards and what they know about food at home. Present findings. Discuss how spices connect to cultural identity.

description.en: Each child names one food from home that uses a spice, and points to where that spice comes from on the world map.
description.es: Each child names one food from home that uses a spice, and points to where that spice comes from on the world map.

sayThis.en: "Think of a food you eat at home. Does it have a spice in it? Which one? Let's find where it comes from on the map."
sayThis.es: "Think of a food you eat at home. Does it have a spice in it? Which one? Let's find where it comes from on the map."

watchFor.en: Children who cannot think of one. Offer pizza, tacos or cinnamon toast.
watchFor.es: Children who cannot think of one. Offer pizza, tacos or cinnamon toast.

doneWhen.en: Every child has named one food from home and its spice.
doneWhen.es: Every child has named one food from home and its spice.

sayThis.en: "Rank them. Most valuable down to least. Not which you like — which you'd pay for. Then tell me why your number one is number one."
sayThis.es: "Rank them. Most valuable down to least. Not which you like — which you'd pay for. Then tell me why your number one is number one."

doneWhen.en: Every group has a written ranking with a reason on the top one.
doneWhen.es: Every group has a written ranking with a reason on the top one.

watchFor.en: Ranking by favorite smell. Push back once: would you hand over money for it?
watchFor.es: Ranking by favorite smell. Push back once: would you hand over money for it?

description.en: Synthesize learning: Why were spices worth traveling thousands of miles? How do spices connect cultures? What determines spice value today vs historically? Write a spice value ranking on scrap paper and justify choices.
description.es: Synthesize learning: Why were spices worth traveling thousands of miles? How do spices connect cultures? What determines spice value today vs historically? Write a spice value ranking on scrap paper and justify choices.

description.en: Each child points to the one spice card they would pay the most for and says why.
description.es: Each child points to the one spice card they would pay the most for and says why.

sayThis.en: "Which spice would you pay the most for? Point to it. Why that one?"
sayThis.es: "Which spice would you pay the most for? Point to it. Why that one?"

watchFor.en: Picking the best smell. Ask once: was it also the hardest card to get?
watchFor.es: Picking the best smell. Ask once: was it also the hardest card to get?

doneWhen.en: Every child has pointed to one spice card and said why.
doneWhen.es: Every child has pointed to one spice card and said why.

discussionQuestions: Which spices were hardest to get? Why?
What happened when a spice was rare and popular?
Was it easier to trade for common spices or rare ones? Why?
How did you decide what to offer or accept in a trade?
Why did spices travel such long distances historically? (Profit!)
How does smell/appearance affect willingness to pay?
What's the relationship between scarcity and price?
extensionIdeas: Research Silk Road and spice trade routes
Calculate: If it costs $1 to buy pepper in India and you sell for $5 here, what's your profit?
Create spice blend recipes and cost them out
At home, with a grown-up, smell two spices from the kitchen and draw them for the class
Write persuasive ad for spice stall

beforeClass.en: Make one spice clue card per station on scrap paper: a crayon drawing of the spice, its color and look, a smell clue, and where it comes from, with the name on the back. Tear small spice cards for the trading game, with only a few of one rare spice, and write an order sheet for each merchant. Hang the world map where everyone can see it.
beforeClass.es: Make one spice clue card per station on scrap paper: a crayon drawing of the spice, its color and look, a smell clue, and where it comes from, with the name on the back. Tear small spice cards for the trading game, with only a few of one rare spice, and write an order sheet for each merchant. Hang the world map where everyone can see it.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: turn the cultural research into one whole-class list. Short: add a clue-only round — read a smell clue with the card face down and have them name the spice.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: turn the cultural research into one whole-class list. Short: add a clue-only round — read a smell clue with the card face down and have them name the spice.

beforeClass.en: Make one spice clue card per station on scrap paper: a crayon drawing of the spice, its color and look, a smell clue, and where it comes from, with the name on the back. Tear small spice cards for the trading game, with only a few of one rare spice, and write an order sheet for each merchant. Draw a simple world map on the board.
beforeClass.es: Make one spice clue card per station on scrap paper: a crayon drawing of the spice, its color and look, a smell clue, and where it comes from, with the name on the back. Tear small spice cards for the trading game, with only a few of one rare spice, and write an order sheet for each merchant. Draw a simple world map on the board.

focus: Focus on smell words and guessing a spice from a clue
Simple sorting (spices I like / spices I don't like)
Basic trading (one-for-one)
Drawing instead of writing descriptions
Vocabulary: smell, spice, trade, like
Descriptive language (sweet, spicy, strong)
Simple comparison (common spices vs. rare ones)
Guided negotiation with teacher support
Basic map work (pointing to continents)
Vocabulary: expensive, cheap, rare, common, market
Detailed sensory descriptions
Understanding value = scarcity
Independent negotiation
Locating countries on map
Vocabulary: scarcity, negotiation, barter, trade route
Scientific observation and recording
Economic analysis (track your trades and profit)
Strategic negotiation
Trade route mapping and cultural research
Advanced vocabulary: merchant, supply, demand, profit, scarcity

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Smell clues need very few words. Teach sweet, spicy, strong and mild with a face or gesture for each.
Invite students to say a spice's name in their home language; many spices have one.
Give the frame: "This smells ___. I will trade ___ for ___."

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Let a student who does not know a smell pair with a partner who does, or sort by the pictures alone.
Use fewer spices, three or four, and let the student draw instead of writing.
Let a student make a trade by pointing to a card instead of talking it out.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Mark on the world map where each spice comes from, and say which traveled farthest.
Explain why a rare spice was worth more, using what happened to the rare card in the trade.
Choose which spice is rare in the trading game, and predict what will happen to its value.

description.en: Explain how auctions work: items for sale, people bid (offer price), highest bid wins. Show the sample bidding paddle. Practice auction calls: 'Going once, going twice, sold!' Each bidder writes $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil.
description.es: Explain how auctions work: items for sale, people bid (offer price), highest bid wins. Show the sample bidding paddle. Practice auction calls: 'Going once, going twice, sold!' Each bidder writes $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil.

sayThis.en: "An auction is a way to sell things. I hold up a thing. You bid — that means you say how much you will pay. The biggest bid wins. Write $20 at the top of your card. That is all your money."
sayThis.es: "An auction is a way to sell things. I hold up a thing. You bid — that means you say how much you will pay. The biggest bid wins. Write $20 at the top of your card. That is all your money."

watchFor.en: Kids who think they can bid more than $20. Say it plainly: when your card says zero, you are done.
watchFor.es: Kids who think they can bid more than $20. Say it plainly: when your card says zero, you are done.

doneWhen.en: Every child has $20 on a card, and the class has said "going once, going twice, sold!" together.
doneWhen.es: Every child has $20 on a card, and the class has said "going once, going twice, sold!" together.

description.en: You hold the money. Give each child a card with $20 already written on it and keep track of what is left yourself. Show the paddle and practice the call together: going once, going twice, sold.
description.es: You hold the money. Give each child a card with $20 already written on it and keep track of what is left yourself. Show the paddle and practice the call together: going once, going twice, sold.

sayThis.en: "An auction is a way to sell things. I hold up a thing. You bid. Bid means you say how much you will pay. The biggest bid wins. Your card says $20. That is all your money, and I keep it for you."
sayThis.es: "An auction is a way to sell things. I hold up a thing. You bid. Bid means you say how much you will pay. The biggest bid wins. Your card says $20. That is all your money, and I keep it for you."

description.en: Display classroom auction items (books, supplies, privileges like line leader). Students preview items and decide what they want most. Plan bidding strategy: save money for favorite item or spread out bids?
description.es: Display classroom auction items (books, supplies, privileges like line leader). Students preview items and decide what they want most. Plan bidding strategy: save money for favorite item or spread out bids?

sayThis.en: "Look at all five things. Which one do you want most? Will you save your money for that one, or try for a few?"
sayThis.es: "Look at all five things. Which one do you want most? Will you save your money for that one, or try for a few?"

watchFor.en: Hands on the items. Look, don't touch; the items stay on the table.
watchFor.es: Hands on the items. Look, don't touch; the items stay on the table.

doneWhen.en: Every child can point to the one item they want most.
doneWhen.es: Every child can point to the one item they want most.

description.en: Show the five auction items (a book, supplies, a privilege like line leader). Children look at each one and pick the one item they want most.
description.es: Show the five auction items (a book, supplies, a privilege like line leader). Children look at each one and pick the one item they want most.

sayThis.en: "Look at all five things. Which one do you want most? Point to it."
sayThis.es: "Look at all five things. Which one do you want most? Point to it."

watchFor.en: Hands on the items. Look, don't touch; the items stay on the table.
watchFor.es: Hands on the items. Look, don't touch; the items stay on the table.

doneWhen.en: Every child can point to the one item they want most.
doneWhen.es: Every child can point to the one item they want most.

description.en: Students fold a piece of scrap paper into a bidding paddle and write their name on it with a pencil. Check the number on their budget card. Review auction rules: raise paddle to bid, teacher/auctioneer decides when sold, you cannot bid more than your card says. Practice raising paddles.
description.es: Students fold a piece of scrap paper into a bidding paddle and write their name on it with a pencil. Check the number on their budget card. Review auction rules: raise paddle to bid, teacher/auctioneer decides when sold, you cannot bid more than your card says. Practice raising paddles.

sayThis.en: "Fold your paper and write your name on it. That's your paddle. Raise it to bid. Check your card: you can't bid more than it says."
sayThis.es: "Fold your paper and write your name on it. That's your paddle. Raise it to bid. Check your card: you can't bid more than it says."

watchFor.en: Paddles waved in a friend's face. Practice once together: paddle up, paddle down.
watchFor.es: Paddles waved in a friend's face. Practice once together: paddle up, paddle down.

doneWhen.en: Every child has a paddle and has practiced raising it.
doneWhen.es: Every child has a paddle and has practiced raising it.

description.en: Skip the paper paddles and the name writing. A raised hand is the bid. Practice it twice together: hand up, hand down.
description.es: Skip the paper paddles and the name writing. A raised hand is the bid. Practice it twice together: hand up, hand down.

sayThis.en: "No paper paddles today. Your hand is your paddle. Hand up means I will pay. Practice with me. Hand up. Hand down."
sayThis.es: "No paper paddles today. Your hand is your paddle. Hand up means I will pay. Practice with me. Hand up. Hand down."

watchFor.en: Hands that go up and never come down. Practice hand up, hand down twice before the first item.
watchFor.es: Hands that go up and never come down. Practice hand up, hand down twice before the first item.

doneWhen.en: Every hand has gone up and come back down twice.
doneWhen.es: Every hand has gone up and come back down twice.

description.en: Run the auction! Auctioneer presents each item. Students bid by raising paddles. Track winning bids on the board. The highest bidder crosses out the number on their budget card, writes what is left, and receives the item.
description.es: Run the auction! Auctioneer presents each item. Students bid by raising paddles. Track winning bids on the board. The highest bidder crosses out the number on their budget card, writes what is left, and receives the item.

sayThis.en: "First thing! Who will pay one dollar? Two dollars? Going once, going twice, sold! Winner, cross out your number and write what's left."
sayThis.es: "First thing! Who will pay one dollar? Two dollars? Going once, going twice, sold! Winner, cross out your number and write what's left."

watchFor.en: Winners who don't take the money off their card. Do the take-away with them on the board.
watchFor.es: Winners who don't take the money off their card. Do the take-away with them on the board.

doneWhen.en: All five items are sold and every winning bid is on the board.
doneWhen.es: All five items are sold and every winning bid is on the board.

description.en: Run the auction. Hold up each item. Children bid by raising their hands, one dollar at a time. Write each winning bid on the board. The teacher counts back what the winner has left and writes it on the winner's card.
description.es: Run the auction. Hold up each item. Children bid by raising their hands, one dollar at a time. Write each winning bid on the board. The teacher counts back what the winner has left and writes it on the winner's card.

sayThis.en: "First thing! Who will pay one dollar? Two dollars? Going once, going twice, sold! I will write on your card how much you have left."
sayThis.es: "First thing! Who will pay one dollar? Two dollars? Going once, going twice, sold! I will write on your card how much you have left."

watchFor.en: Kids bidding more than their card says. Point to the number on the card and count up to it together.
watchFor.es: Kids bidding more than their card says. Point to the number on the card and count up to it together.

doneWhen.en: All five items are sold, every winning bid is on the board, and every winner's card shows what is left.
doneWhen.es: All five items are sold, every winning bid is on the board, and every winner's card shows what is left.

description.en: Discuss: What sold for the most? Why? Did you get what you wanted? What happens when many people want the same thing? How is an auction different from a regular store?
description.es: Discuss: What sold for the most? Why? Did you get what you wanted? What happens when many people want the same thing? How is an auction different from a regular store?

sayThis.en: "What sold for the most? Why do you think so many people wanted it?"
sayThis.es: "What sold for the most? Why do you think so many people wanted it?"

watchFor.en: Kids upset they won nothing. Say that keeping your money is a choice too.
watchFor.es: Kids upset they won nothing. Say that keeping your money is a choice too.

doneWhen.en: Two children have said why the top item went so high.
doneWhen.es: Two children have said why the top item went so high.

description.en: One question only: which thing sold for the most money? Skip the questions about wanting the same thing and about stores.
description.es: One question only: which thing sold for the most money? Skip the questions about wanting the same thing and about stores.

doneWhen.en: Two children have pointed at the thing that sold for the most.
doneWhen.es: Two children have pointed at the thing that sold for the most.

discussionQuestions: What item sold for the most? Why?
Did you spend your money wisely?
What happens when lots of people want the same thing?

beforeClass.en: Pick five items or privileges from the room to auction, like a book, a pencil, or line leader for a day. Make one sample paddle from scrap paper to show. Cut a scrap-paper budget card for every student with scissors.
beforeClass.es: Pick five items or privileges from the room to auction, like a book, a pencil, or line leader for a day. Make one sample paddle from scrap paper to show. Cut a scrap-paper budget card for every student with scissors.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: end Item Preview & Bidding Planning early once every child has pointed to the item they want most. Short: in the Classroom Auction, let a volunteer be the auctioneer for the last item.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: end Item Preview & Bidding Planning early once every child has pointed to the item they want most. Short: in the Classroom Auction, let a volunteer be the auctioneer for the last item.

description.en: Each student writes $50 on a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil as their starting balance - Display all 10 items so students can plan - Explain bidding: "Start at $5. You can bid higher. Highest bidder wins." - Introduce budget tracking sheet: record each purchase.
description.es: Each student writes $50 on a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil as their starting balance - Display all 10 items so students can plan - Explain bidding: "Start at $5. You can bid higher. Highest bidder wins." - Introduce budget tracking sheet: record each purchase.

sayThis.en: "Write $50 at the top of your card. That's all your money today. Look at the ten things. Bidding starts at five dollars. Every time you win, write what you bought and what you paid on your sheet."
sayThis.es: "Write $50 at the top of your card. That's all your money today. Look at the ten things. Bidding starts at five dollars. Every time you win, write what you bought and what you paid on your sheet."

watchFor.en: Kids planning to spend all fifty on the first item. Ask what they'll do when their favorite comes up later.
watchFor.es: Kids planning to spend all fifty on the first item. Ask what they'll do when their favorite comes up later.

doneWhen.en: Every student has $50 on a card and a tracking sheet ready.
doneWhen.es: Every student has $50 on a card and a tracking sheet ready.

description.en: Each child writes $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil. That is all their money. Show all 10 items. Explain bidding: start at $1, go up one dollar at a time, and the biggest bid wins. Show the tracking sheet: draw each thing you win.
description.es: Each child writes $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil. That is all their money. Show all 10 items. Explain bidding: start at $1, go up one dollar at a time, and the biggest bid wins. Show the tracking sheet: draw each thing you win.

sayThis.en: "Write $20 at the top of your card. That's all your money today. Look at the ten things. Bidding starts at one dollar. When you win, draw what you got on your sheet."
sayThis.es: "Write $20 at the top of your card. That's all your money today. Look at the ten things. Bidding starts at one dollar. When you win, draw what you got on your sheet."

watchFor.en: Kids planning to spend all twenty on the first item. Ask what they will do when their favorite comes up later.
watchFor.es: Kids planning to spend all twenty on the first item. Ask what they will do when their favorite comes up later.

doneWhen.en: Every child has $20 on a card and a tracking sheet ready.
doneWhen.es: Every child has $20 on a card and a tracking sheet ready.

description.en: Auction 5 items - After each sale, pause: "How much money do you have left?" - Students record purchases on tracking sheet.
description.es: Auction 5 items - After each sale, pause: "How much money do you have left?" - Students record purchases on tracking sheet.

sayThis.en: "First item. Five dollars? Ten? Going once, going twice, sold! Stop. Winner, write it down. Everyone: how much money do you have left?"
sayThis.es: "First item. Five dollars? Ten? Going once, going twice, sold! Stop. Winner, write it down. Everyone: how much money do you have left?"

watchFor.en: Winners forgetting to take the bid off their card. Wait after each sale until the winner's card is updated.
watchFor.es: Winners forgetting to take the bid off their card. Wait after each sale until the winner's card is updated.

doneWhen.en: Five items are sold and every winner has a new number on their card.
doneWhen.es: Five items are sold and every winner has a new number on their card.

description.en: Auction 5 items, one dollar at a time. After each sale, stop. The teacher counts back what the winner has left and writes it on the winner's card. The winner draws the item on the tracking sheet.
description.es: Auction 5 items, one dollar at a time. After each sale, stop. The teacher counts back what the winner has left and writes it on the winner's card. The winner draws the item on the tracking sheet.

sayThis.en: "First item. One dollar? Two? Going once, going twice, sold! Stop. Winner, draw it on your sheet. I will write how much money you have left."
sayThis.es: "First item. One dollar? Two? Going once, going twice, sold! Stop. Winner, draw it on your sheet. I will write how much money you have left."

watchFor.en: Winners who want to bid again before their card is done. Wait after each sale until you have written the new number.
watchFor.es: Winners who want to bid again before their card is done. Wait after each sale until you have written the new number.

doneWhen.en: Five items are sold and every winner has a new number on their card.
doneWhen.es: Five items are sold and every winner has a new number on their card.

description.en: "What have you noticed? What's your strategy for the remaining items?"
description.es: "What have you noticed? What's your strategy for the remaining items?"

sayThis.en: "What have you noticed? Who's running low? What's your plan for the last five things?"
sayThis.es: "What have you noticed? Who's running low? What's your plan for the last five things?"

watchFor.en: Only the loud kids answering. Ask one student with lots left and one with a little what they'll do.
watchFor.es: Only the loud kids answering. Ask one student with lots left and one with a little what they'll do.

doneWhen.en: Three students have said their plan for the second half.
doneWhen.es: Three students have said their plan for the second half.

description.en: Auction final 5 items (include some "surprise" items — mystery bags) - Watch for strategic behavior: saving vs. spending
description.es: Auction final 5 items (include some "surprise" items — mystery bags) - Watch for strategic behavior: saving vs. spending

sayThis.en: "Last five things. Some are mystery bags. You can't see inside. How much is a maybe worth?"
sayThis.es: "Last five things. Some are mystery bags. You can't see inside. How much is a maybe worth?"

watchFor.en: Nobody bidding on a mystery bag. Open at one dollar to get it moving.
watchFor.es: Nobody bidding on a mystery bag. Open at one dollar to get it moving.

doneWhen.en: All ten items are sold and the mystery bags are opened.
doneWhen.es: All ten items are sold and the mystery bags are opened.

description.en: Count: Who spent all money? Who saved some? - Discuss: Which items went for highest prices? Why? - Graph: Actual sale prices vs. teacher's guess
description.es: Count: Who spent all money? Who saved some? - Discuss: Which items went for highest prices? Why? - Graph: Actual sale prices vs. teacher's guess

sayThis.en: "Hands up if you spent all your money. Hands up if you saved some. Here is my guess for each price. Were you higher or lower?"
sayThis.es: "Hands up if you spent all your money. Hands up if you saved some. Here is my guess for each price. Were you higher or lower?"

watchFor.en: Running out of time for the graph. Draw bars for the two highest items only.
watchFor.es: Running out of time for the graph. Draw bars for the two highest items only.

doneWhen.en: Sale prices and your guesses are side by side on the board.
doneWhen.es: Sale prices and your guesses are side by side on the board.

discussionQuestions: What was your strategy?
Did you run out of money before getting something you wanted?
What would you do differently next time?
How did competition affect prices?
extensionIdeas: Students calculate "satisfaction rating" for purchases - did high-priced items make them happier?

sayThis.es: "One hundred dollars on your card. That is all the money you will ever have today. Go through the catalogue and write the most you'd pay for each thing. Write it now, before the bidding, because once it starts you'll want everything."

doneWhen.en: Every budget card shows $100 and a maximum written beside at least five lots.
doneWhen.es: Every budget card shows $100 and a maximum written beside at least five lots.

watchFor.en: A maximum of one hundred written on every line. Ask what they'll bid with on lot two.

description.en: Students write $100 on their scrap-paper budget card with a pencil and take an auction catalog - Students review all items and plan strategy - Budget worksheet: rank items by desire, set maximum bid for each - Discuss: opportunity cost ("If you spend $40 on Item 1, what can't you buy?") - Introduce roles: some students will be bidders, others will be auctioneer's assistants (tracking prices).
description.es: Students write $100 on their scrap-paper budget card with a pencil and take an auction catalog - Students review all items and plan strategy - Budget worksheet: rank items by desire, set maximum bid for each - Discuss: opportunity cost ("If you spend $40 on Item 1, what can't you buy?") - Introduce roles: some students will be bidders, others will be auctioneer's assistants (tracking prices).

description.en: Children write $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil. Look through the table catalogue together. Each child circles the one item they want most. Talk about it: if you spend all your money on one thing, you cannot buy another. Some children will be bidders; a few will be the auctioneer's helpers.
description.es: Children write $20 at the top of a scrap-paper budget card with a pencil. Look through the table catalogue together. Each child circles the one item they want most. sayThis.en: "Twenty dollars on your card. That is all your money today. Look at the catalogue. Circle the one thing you want most. If you spend it all on one thing, you can't buy anything else."
sayThis.es: "Twenty dollars on your card. That is all your money today. Look at the catalogue. Circle the one thing you want most. If you spend it all on one thing, you can't buy anything else."

watchFor.en: Children circling everything. Ask: if you could take home only one, which one?
watchFor.es: Children circling everything. Ask: if you could take home only one, which one?

doneWhen.en: Every budget card shows $20 and every child has circled one item.
doneWhen.es: Every budget card shows $20 and every child has circled one item.

sayThis.en: "Hand up to bid. If you bid and you win, you pay. Do I hear five? Ten? Going once — going twice — sold to number seven."
sayThis.es: "Hand up to bid. If you bid and you win, you pay. Do I hear five? Ten? Going once — going twice — sold to number seven."

doneWhen.en: Five lots are sold and each winning price is on the chart.
doneWhen.es: Five lots are sold and each winning price is on the chart.

watchFor.en: Winners who forget to subtract. Stop after every second lot and make the whole room update the card.
watchFor.es: Winners who forget to subtract. Stop after every second lot and make the whole room update the card.

description.en: Auction first 5 items - Teacher as auctioneer: "Do I hear $5? $10? Going once, going twice, SOLD to bidder #7!" - Assistants record winning bids on chart - After each sale, brief pause for students to update budgets
description.es: Auction first 5 items - Teacher as auctioneer: "Do I hear $5? $10? Going once, going twice, SOLD to bidder #7!" - Assistants record winning bids on chart - After each sale, brief pause for students to update budgets

description.en: Auction the first 5 items, one dollar at a time. The teacher is the auctioneer: "Do I hear one dollar? Two? Going once, going twice, sold to bidder number 7!" Helpers point to where the winning bid goes on the board chart. After each sale, the teacher counts back what the winner has left and writes it on the winner's card.
description.es: Auction the first 5 items, one dollar at a time. The teacher is the auctioneer: "Do I hear one dollar? Two? Going once, going twice, sold to bidder number 7!" sayThis.en: "Hand up to bid. If you bid and you win, you pay. Do I hear one dollar? Two? Going once, going twice, sold to number seven. I'll write what you have left on your card."
sayThis.es: "Hand up to bid. If you bid and you win, you pay. Do I hear one dollar? Two? Going once, going twice, sold to number seven. I'll write what you have left on your card."

watchFor.en: Winners bidding again before their card is done. Stop after each sale until you have written the new number.
watchFor.es: Winners bidding again before their card is done. Stop after each sale until you have written the new number.

doneWhen.en: Five lots are sold, each winning price is on the chart, and every winner's card shows what is left.
doneWhen.es: Five lots are sold, each winning price is on the chart, and every winner's card shows what is left.

sayThis.en: "Five prices up there. Which went high? Was it the best thing, or the thing the most people wanted? Hands up if you've got less than thirty dollars left."
sayThis.es: "Five prices up there. Which went high? Was it the best thing, or the thing the most people wanted? Hands up if you've got less than thirty dollars left."

doneWhen.en: The five prices are charted and the number of students under $30 is counted out loud.
doneWhen.es: The five prices are charted and the number of students under $30 is counted out loud.

watchFor.en: "It's just the best one" with nothing behind it. Point at two lots that went for the same money and look nothing alike.
watchFor.es: "It's just the best one" with nothing behind it. Point at two lots that went for the same money and look nothing alike.

description.en: Chart first 5 prices - Discuss: "What patterns do you see? Which items went high? Why?" - "How many of you are running low on money?" - Introduce concepts: bidding war, market value, reserve price
description.es: Chart first 5 prices - Discuss: "What patterns do you see? Which items went high? Why?" - "How many of you are running low on money?" - Introduce concepts: bidding war, market value, reserve price

description.en: Point to the first 5 prices on the board chart. Ask: which things went high? Why? Who is running low on money? Teach one new word: a bidding war is when lots of people want the same thing and keep bidding.
description.es: Point to the first 5 prices on the board chart. Ask: which things went high? Why? Who is running low on money? Teach one new word: a bidding war is when lots of people want the same thing and keep bidding.

sayThis.en: "Five prices up there. Which one went highest? Was it the best thing, or the thing the most people wanted? Hands up if your card says less than five dollars."
sayThis.es: "Five prices up there. Which one went highest? Was it the best thing, or the thing the most people wanted? Hands up if your card says less than five dollars."

watchFor.en: "It's just the best one" with nothing behind it. Ask how many hands went up for that one.
watchFor.es: "It's just the best one" with nothing behind it. Ask how many hands went up for that one.

doneWhen.en: The five prices are on the chart and the class has counted who has less than $5 left.
doneWhen.es: The five prices are on the chart and the class has counted who has less than $5 left.

sayThis.en: "You can't see inside. You bid anyway. So — what's a maybe worth?"
sayThis.es: "You can't see inside. You bid anyway. So — what's a maybe worth?"

doneWhen.en: All three mystery lots are sold, opened and held up for the room.
doneWhen.es: All three mystery lots are sold, opened and held up for the room.

watchFor.en: Nobody bidding at all. Open at one dollar to get it moving.
watchFor.es: Nobody bidding at all. Open at one dollar to get it moving.

description.en: Include 3 mystery bags/boxes (unknown contents) - Students must bid blind - Discuss: "How do you decide value when you don't know what's inside?" - Unwrap after bidding - discuss willingness to take risks
description.es: Include 3 mystery bags/boxes (unknown contents) - Students must bid blind - Discuss: "How do you decide value when you don't know what's inside?" - Unwrap after bidding - discuss willingness to take risks

sayThis.en: "You run it now. Take a bid, say it back louder, ask for more. Then going once, going twice, sold."
sayThis.es: "You run it now. Take a bid, say it back louder, ask for more. Then going once, going twice, sold."

doneWhen.en: Every remaining lot has been sold by a student auctioneer.
doneWhen.es: Every remaining lot has been sold by a student auctioneer.

watchFor.en: A quiet auctioneer losing the room. Stand beside them and repeat the bids for the first lot.
watchFor.es: A quiet auctioneer losing the room. Stand beside them and repeat the bids for the first lot.

description.en: Volunteer students take over as auctioneers - Final items auctioned - Observe strategic behavior: desperation bidding, saving, bargain hunting
description.es: Volunteer students take over as auctioneers - Final items auctioned - Observe strategic behavior: desperation bidding, saving, bargain hunting

sayThis.en: "Every lot and every price on the graph. Highest. Lowest. Now — who's still got money, and did they lose out, or did they play it smarter?"
sayThis.es: "Every lot and every price on the graph. Highest. Lowest. Now — who's still got money, and did they lose out, or did they play it smarter?"

doneWhen.en: The bar graph is drawn and the highest and lowest prices are circled.
doneWhen.es: The bar graph is drawn and the highest and lowest prices are circled.

watchFor.en: Winner-takes-all framing. Ask the student with cash left what they chose not to buy.
watchFor.es: Winner-takes-all framing. Ask the student with cash left what they chose not to buy.

description.en: Create bar graph: all items and their final prices - Calculate: average price, highest price, lowest price - Discuss findings: - "Did expensive items make people happier?" - "What determined final price: actual value or how much people wanted it?" - "What's the difference between what something costs and what it's worth?" - "Who managed their budget best? How?"
description.es: Create bar graph: all items and their final prices - Calculate: average price, highest price, lowest price - Discuss findings: - "Did expensive items make people happier?" - "What determined final price: actual value or how much people wanted it?" - "What's the difference between what something costs and what it's worth?" - "Who managed their budget best? How?"

description.en: Draw a bar graph on the board: one bar for each item and its price. Find the highest price and the lowest price. Ask: did the most expensive thing make someone the happiest? Who still has money, and what did they choose not to buy?
description.es: Draw a bar graph on the board: one bar for each item and its price. Find the highest price and the lowest price. Ask: did the most expensive thing make someone the happiest? Who still has money, and what did they choose not to buy?

sayThis.en: "Every item and every price on the graph. Which bar is the tallest? Which is the shortest? Who still has money left? Was that a smart choice?"
sayThis.es: "Every item and every price on the graph. Which bar is the tallest? Which is the shortest? Who still has money left? Was that a smart choice?"

watchFor.en: Children who won nothing feeling bad. Say that keeping your money is a choice too.
watchFor.es: Children who won nothing feeling bad. Say that keeping your money is a choice too.

doneWhen.en: The bar graph is drawn and the highest and lowest prices are circled.
doneWhen.es: The bar graph is drawn and the highest and lowest prices are circled.

discussionQuestions: What was your bidding strategy? Did it work?
Did you change your strategy during the auction? Why?
What happens when people compete for the same item?
Is the highest-priced item always the best? Why or why not?
How does an auction determine the 'true' value of something?
When might auctions be better than fixed prices? When might fixed prices be better?
What emotions did you feel during bidding?
How did you decide when to stop bidding on something?
extensionIdeas: Students sell their own items in a second auction
Research real auctions (art, antiques, livestock, online)
Calculate: if you could return items for refund, which would you return?
Write reflection: "The most important thing I learned about money and value"
Compare auction prices to "store prices" - which would you choose and why?

beforeClass.en: Lay the lots out (books, supplies or privileges from the room) where they can be seen and not handled, and number them. Write the catalogue by hand on scrap paper, one copy per table. Choose your three mystery lots now, put each in a paper bag or box from home, and make sure what's inside is worth winning — a disappointing mystery bag kills the next round.
beforeClass.es: Lay the lots out (books, supplies or privileges from the room) where they can be seen and not handled, and number them. Write the catalogue by hand on scrap paper, one copy per table. runningLongOrShort.en: Long: cut the student auctioneer round to two lots. Short: add a final lot and let everyone bid whatever they have left.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: cut the student auctioneer round to two lots. Short: add a final lot and let everyone bid whatever they have left.

focus: Very simple budget ($10-20)

Teacher tracks money for students

Guided budget tracking with help
Basic strategy discussion
Vocabulary: budget, spend, save, price, highest bidder
Full budget ($50-100)
Independent money management
Written budget planning
Understanding of opportunity cost
Vocabulary: opportunity cost, market value, strategy, competition
Complex budget scenarios

Data analysis of auction results
Advanced economic concepts

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Show a bid with a paddle and fingers for the dollar amount, so no words are needed.
Picture the items on the board with a number for each, so students can bid by item number.
Teach four words with gestures before starting: bid, sold, money, left.

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Before the auction, help the student pick two or three items to focus on.
Give the student a buddy or the teacher to keep their budget card up to date.
Give extra think time before each lot: count to five before you take the first bid.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Be the auctioneer's assistant: record every winning bid and each winner's money left.
Take a turn as auctioneer and explain afterward why some items went higher than expected.
Write the catalog: a one-line description and a starting bid for each item.

fromScratch.costPerStudent: $0 — everything is free or from home
fromScratch.description: Everything is free: cardboard boxes and old magazines for the pastry parts, newspaper wraps, tape, paper-strip rulers, scrap paper for cost sheets, labels and price tags, crayons, pencils, and the board.
items: Cardboard boxes — 5, from home, free, flattened, one per team for the pastry bases
Magazines — 5 old ones, free, one per team, pages for the frosting layers and the paper ties
Newspaper — 5 sheets, free, one per team, to wrap the finished pastries
Tape — 5 rolls, one per team, to hold the parts together
Paper-strip rulers — 5, one per team, strips of scrap paper about one foot long, free
Scrap paper — 30 pieces, free, parts cost sheets, worksheets, labels and price tags
Crayons — 5 boxes, one per team, for price tags and the bakery logo
Pencils — 5, one per team, for the tally and the worksheet
Board — teacher, for the party-shop prices and each team's price and profit
Calculator — the teacher's phone, free, for a student who needs help with the adding and dividing (accommodation)

items: Cardstock — 10 sheets, two per team for 5 teams, for the pastry bases
