sayThis.en: "A stand on paper, and we're going to find every single thing it costs. Not just the obvious ones. Four words to know: revenue is what comes in, expenses go out, overhead is what you pay whether you sell anything or not, and profit is what's actually left. Before we start, write down your guess: how much profit does this stand make?"
sayThis.es: "A stand on paper, and we're going to find every single thing it costs. Not just the obvious ones. Four words to know: revenue is what comes in, expenses go out, overhead is what you pay whether you sell anything or not, and profit is what's actually left. Before we start, write down your guess: how much profit does this stand make?"

doneWhen.en: All four terms are on the board with a one-line meaning each, and every student has written a profit guess.
doneWhen.es: All four terms are on the board with a one-line meaning each, and every student has written a profit guess.

watchFor.en: Overhead being skipped as a hard word. Give an example: you pay for the table even if nobody buys.
watchFor.es: Overhead being skipped as a hard word. Give an example: you pay for the table even if nobody buys.

description.en: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit. Each student writes down a quick guess of the stand's profit.
description.es: Introduce detailed lemonade stand scenario with price list. Students will track ALL costs including ones people forget. Review terms: revenue, expenses, overhead, profit. Each student writes down a quick guess of the stand's profit.

description.en: Show the $10 lemonade stand on the board: 10 cups sold at $1 each. Teach three words with a quick drawing for each: money in, costs and profit. Profit is the money left after you pay the costs. Every student guesses with fingers how many of the 10 dollars the stand keeps.
description.es: Show the $10 lemonade stand on the board: 10 cups sold at $1 each. Teach three words with a quick drawing for each: money in, costs and profit. Profit is the money left after you pay the costs. Every student guesses with fingers how many of the 10 dollars the stand keeps.

sayThis.en: "Our stand sold 10 cups for $1 each. That is $10 of money in. But the stand had to pay for things. Those are costs. What is left is profit. Hold up fingers: how many dollars do you think we keep?"
sayThis.es: "Our stand sold 10 cups for $1 each. That is $10 of money in. But the stand had to pay for things. Those are costs. What is left is profit. Hold up fingers: how many dollars do you think we keep?"

watchFor.en: Ten fingers from almost everyone. Don't correct it. Write the guesses on the board and come back to them at the end.
watchFor.es: Ten fingers from almost everyone. Don't correct it. Write the guesses on the board and come back to them at the end.

doneWhen.en: Money in, costs and profit are on the board with a drawing each, and the finger guesses are written down.
doneWhen.es: Money in, costs and profit are on the board with a drawing each, and the finger guesses are written down.

sayThis.en: "Three buckets. Direct costs are the things that become the product. Overhead is what you pay anyway. Labor is your own time, and your time is not free. Fill all three."
sayThis.es: "Three buckets. Direct costs are the things that become the product. Overhead is what you pay anyway. Labor is your own time, and your time is not free. Fill all three."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has at least two items listed in all three categories.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has at least two items listed in all three categories.

watchFor.en: Empty labor columns. Ask what they'd charge someone else to stand there for two hours.
watchFor.es: Empty labor columns. Ask what they'd charge someone else to stand there for two hours.

description.en: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.
description.es: Break costs into categories: Direct costs (lemons, sugar, cups), Overhead (table rental, sign materials), Labor (your time). Students brainstorm items in each category.

description.en: Draw three circles on the board: Things in the Cup, Things for the Stand, and Our Time. Students name things the stand needs, and the class decides which circle each one goes in. Draw a quick picture beside each.
description.es: Draw three circles on the board: Things in the Cup, Things for the Stand, and Our Time. Students name things the stand needs, and the class decides which circle each one goes in. Draw a quick picture beside each.

sayThis.en: "What goes in the cup? Lemons. What else? What does the stand need? A table. A sign. And who stands there all afternoon? You do. Your time counts too."
sayThis.es: "What goes in the cup? Lemons. What else? What does the stand need? A table. A sign. And who stands there all afternoon? You do. Your time counts too."

watchFor.en: An empty Our Time circle. Ask "Would you stand there all afternoon for nothing?"
watchFor.es: An empty Our Time circle. Ask "Would you stand there all afternoon for nothing?"

doneWhen.en: Each of the three circles on the board has at least two things in it.
doneWhen.es: Each of the three circles on the board has at least two things in it.

sayThis.en: "Real numbers off the price sheet now, not guesses. Add up each bucket separately, then all three together. That total is what it cost before a single sale."
sayThis.es: "Real numbers off the price sheet now, not guesses. Add up each bucket separately, then all three together. That total is what it cost before a single sale."

doneWhen.en: Every pair has three category totals and a grand total written down.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has three category totals and a grand total written down.

watchFor.en: Pairs adding everything into one pile. The three separate totals are what makes the next steps work.
watchFor.es: Pairs adding everything into one pile. The three separate totals are what makes the next steps work.

description.en: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using the price sheet on the board. Price only items that are on the sheet, and use the hourly labor rate for your time. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record on your cost sheet.
description.es: In pairs, students estimate real costs for each item using the price sheet on the board. Price only items that are on the sheet, and use the hourly labor rate for your time. Calculate total direct costs, total overhead, total labor. Record on your cost sheet.

description.en: The teacher writes the price from the price list beside each thing in the three circles. Things not on the price list cost nothing today. In pairs, students count the dollars in one circle on their fingers, then the class counts each circle together. The teacher writes each circle's dollars beside it.
description.es: The teacher writes the price from the price list beside each thing in the three circles. Things not on the price list cost nothing today. In pairs, students count the dollars in one circle on their fingers, then the class counts each circle together. The teacher writes each circle's dollars beside it.

sayThis.en: "Our lemons for today cost $2. Sugar costs $1. Count with me: how many dollars are in this circle? Now you and your partner count the next circle."
sayThis.es: "Our lemons for today cost $2. Sugar costs $1. Count with me: how many dollars are in this circle? Now you and your partner count the next circle."

watchFor.en: Pairs counting the things, not the dollars. Point to each price and hold up one finger for each dollar.
watchFor.es: Pairs counting the things, not the dollars. Point to each price and hold up one finger for each dollar.

doneWhen.en: Each circle on the board has its dollars counted and written beside it.
doneWhen.es: Each circle on the board has its dollars counted and written beside it.

sayThis.en: "Ten bought one at a time, against a pack of ten. Work out the saving. Then the catch — you need all the money up front, and whatever you don't use is wasted."
sayThis.es: "Ten bought one at a time, against a pack of ten. Work out the saving. Then the catch — you need all the money up front, and whatever you don't use is wasted."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows both prices and the saving calculated.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows both prices and the saving calculated.

watchFor.en: Bulk treated as always better. Ask what happens if they only sell three.
watchFor.es: Bulk treated as always better. Ask what happens if they only sell three.

description.en: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. a pack of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra).
description.es: Compare costs: buying 10 lemons individually vs. a pack of 10. Calculate savings. Discuss: Why is bulk cheaper? What's the catch? (need money upfront, might waste extra).

description.en: Our price list had $2 of lemons, just enough for one day. Now a new question: write two prices on the board. 10 lemons bought one at a time cost $10, and a pack of 10 lemons costs $6. Students point to the price that costs less. Then ask what happens if the stand only uses 3 lemons.
description.es: Our price list had $2 of lemons, just enough for one day. Now a new question: write two prices on the board. 10 lemons bought one at a time cost $10, and a pack of 10 lemons costs $6. Students point to the price that costs less. Then ask what happens if the stand only uses 3 lemons.

sayThis.en: "Our lemons for one day cost $2. Here is a new question. Ten lemons one at a time cost $10. A pack of ten costs $6. Which one costs less? Now, what if we only use three lemons? What happens to the rest?"
sayThis.es: "Our lemons for one day cost $2. Here is a new question. Ten lemons one at a time cost $10. A pack of ten costs $6. Which one costs less? Now, what if we only use three lemons? What happens to the rest?"

watchFor.en: Students who say the pack is always better. Ask "What if the extra lemons go bad before we use them?"
watchFor.es: Students who say the pack is always better. Ask "What if the extra lemons go bad before we use them?"

doneWhen.en: The class has picked the lower price and named one catch, like extra lemons going to waste.
doneWhen.es: The class has picked the lower price and named one catch, like extra lemons going to waste.

sayThis.en: "Design the sheet you'd actually use. Columns for supplies, time and overhead. Simple enough that you'd fill it in when you're tired, because that's when people stop."
sayThis.es: "Design the sheet you'd actually use. Columns for supplies, time and overhead. Simple enough that you'd fill it in when you're tired, because that's when people stop."

doneWhen.en: Every tracking sheet has been designed and test-filled with at least three rows.
doneWhen.es: Every tracking sheet has been designed and test-filled with at least three rows.

watchFor.en: Beautiful sheets with no room to write. Ask them to fill in three rows of their own design.
watchFor.es: Beautiful sheets with no room to write. Ask them to fill in three rows of their own design.

description.en: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.
description.es: Students design a simple tracking sheet to log hidden costs. Categories: Supplies, Time, Overhead. Practice filling it out for lemonade stand.

description.en: Each student folds a sheet of plain paper into three parts and draws a small picture label in each: a cup, a stand and a smiling face for our time. With a pencil, they draw or write one cost from the board in each part.
description.es: Each student folds a sheet of plain paper into three parts and draws a small picture label in each: a cup, a stand and a smiling face for our time. With a pencil, they draw or write one cost from the board in each part.

sayThis.en: "Fold your paper into three parts. Draw a cup at the top of the first part, a stand in the second, and a smiling face for our time in the third. Now put one cost from the board in each part."
sayThis.es: "Fold your paper into three parts. Draw a cup at the top of the first part, a stand in the second, and a smiling face for our time in the third. Now put one cost from the board in each part."

watchFor.en: Big drawings that fill a whole part. Show a small picture at the top so there is room for the cost.
watchFor.es: Big drawings that fill a whole part. Show a small picture at the top so there is room for the cost.

doneWhen.en: Every sheet has three picture labels and one cost in each part.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet has three picture labels and one cost in each part.

sayThis.en: "Revenue, take off direct costs, take off overhead, take off your own time. What's left? Now compare that to what you guessed at the start. Most people guess about double."
sayThis.es: "Revenue, take off direct costs, take off overhead, take off your own time. What's left? Now compare that to what you guessed at the start. Most people guess about double."

doneWhen.en: Every sheet shows the full subtraction with labor included and the original guess beside it.
doneWhen.es: Every sheet shows the full subtraction with labor included and the original guess beside it.

watchFor.en: Labor quietly dropped to make the profit look better. That's the exact habit this chapter exists to break.
watchFor.es: Labor quietly dropped to make the profit look better. That's the exact habit this chapter exists to break.

description.en: Calculate final profit: Revenue − Direct Costs − Overhead − Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?
description.es: Calculate final profit: Revenue − Direct Costs − Overhead − Labor = Profit. Compare to original guess. Discuss: What surprised you? How can businesses reduce hidden costs?

description.en: Lay out 10 paper clips for the $10 that came in. For each circle on the board, take away one clip for each dollar it costs, and do not skip Our Time. Count the clips that are left. That is the profit. Compare it with the finger guesses from the start, then ask: What surprised you? How could the stand spend less?
description.es: Lay out 10 paper clips for the $10 that came in. For each circle on the board, take away one clip for each dollar it costs, and do not skip Our Time. Count the clips that are left. That is the profit. Compare it with the finger guesses from the start, then ask: What surprised you? How could the stand spend less?

sayThis.en: "Here is our $10. Ten clips. Take away a clip for every dollar in the first circle. Now the stand circle. Now our time. Count what is left. That is our profit. Is it more or less than you guessed?"
sayThis.es: "Here is our $10. Ten clips. Take away a clip for every dollar in the first circle. Now the stand circle. Now our time. Count what is left. That is our profit. Is it more or less than you guessed?"

watchFor.en: The Our Time circle being skipped so more clips are left. Take those clips away too. Time is a cost.
watchFor.es: The Our Time circle being skipped so more clips are left. Take those clips away too. Time is a cost.

doneWhen.en: The clips that are left are counted, the profit is on the board beside the finger guesses, and the class has named one surprise.
doneWhen.es: The clips that are left are counted, the profit is on the board beside the finger guesses, and the class has named one surprise.

description.en: Lay out 10 scrap-paper squares for the $10 that came in. For each circle on the board, take away one square for each dollar it costs, and do not skip Our Time. Count the squares that are left. That is the profit. Compare it with the finger guesses from the start, then ask: What surprised you? How could the stand spend less?
description.es: Lay out 10 scrap-paper squares for the $10 that came in. For each circle on the board, take away one square for each dollar it costs, and do not skip Our Time. Count the squares that are left. That is the profit. Compare it with the finger guesses from the start, then ask: What surprised you? How could the stand spend less?

sayThis.en: "Here is our $10. Ten paper squares. Take away a square for every dollar in the first circle. Now the stand circle. Now our time. Count what is left. That is our profit. Is it more or less than you guessed?"
sayThis.es: "Here is our $10. Ten paper squares. Take away a square for every dollar in the first circle. Now the stand circle. Now our time. Count what is left. That is our profit. Is it more or less than you guessed?"

watchFor.en: The Our Time circle being skipped so more squares are left. Take those squares away too. Time is a cost.
watchFor.es: The Our Time circle being skipped so more squares are left. Take those squares away too. Time is a cost.

doneWhen.en: The squares that are left are counted, the profit is on the board beside the finger guesses, and the class has named one surprise.
doneWhen.es: The squares that are left are counted, the profit is on the board beside the finger guesses, and the class has named one surprise.

discussionQuestions: What's the difference between overhead and material costs?
What does the lemonade stand still pay for on a day when nobody buys a cup?
How does bulk buying change your true cost over time?
What happens to businesses that don't count hidden costs?
Is it 'bad' to discover hidden costs? Or is it helpful to know the truth?
How much overhead should we add to our prices? 10%? 20%? How do we decide?
extensionIdeas: Track a week of classroom hidden costs (markers that dry out, paper waste, electricity for lights)
Research real business overhead percentages by industry (restaurants 30-40%, retail 20-30%)
Create a "Reserve Fund Calculator" for different business scenarios
Visit a local business and interview owner about their overhead costs
Calculate true cost of a school fundraiser (bake sale, car wash, etc.)

beforeClass.en: Write the price sheet on the board: the price of a cup, how many cups the stand sells, a price for every cost item, an hourly rate for labor, and a price for one lemon and for a pack of 10 lemons. Check every item has a number; a missing price stalls a whole pair. Set out plain paper and a pencil for each student. This is a costing exercise on paper — no drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.
beforeClass.es: Write the price sheet on the board: the price of a cup, how many cups the stand sells, a price for every cost item, an hourly rate for labor, and a price for one lemon and for a pack of 10 lemons. Check every item has a number; a missing price stalls a whole pair. Set out plain paper and a pencil for each student. This is a costing exercise on paper — no drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: do the bulk-buying comparison as one whole-class example. Short: add a second scenario with a rainy day and half the customers.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: do the bulk-buying comparison as one whole-class example. Short: add a second scenario with a rainy day and half the customers.

beforeClass.en: Write a $10 stand on the board: 10 cups sold at $1 each. Write this price list too. Things in the Cup: lemons for one day $2, sugar $1. Things for the Stand: cups $1, table $1, sign $1. Our Time: making it $1, selling it $1. That is $8 of costs, so 2 dollars are left. Set out plain paper and a pencil for each student, and have 10 paper clips ready to show the $10. No drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.
beforeClass.es: Write a $10 stand on the board: 10 cups sold at $1 each. Write this price list too. Things in the Cup: lemons for one day $2, sugar $1. Things for the Stand: cups $1, table $1, sign $1. Our Time: making it $1, selling it $1. That is $8 of costs, so 2 dollars are left. Set out plain paper and a pencil for each student, and have 10 paper clips ready to show the $10. No drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: do the cheaper-pack question together as one class. Short: add a rainy day when only 5 cups sell, so $5 comes in. Take away the same costs until the money runs out, then stop. The stand lost money that day, and that is a real answer.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: do the cheaper-pack question together as one class. Short: add a rainy day when only 5 cups sell, so $5 comes in. Take away the same costs until the money runs out, then stop. The stand lost money that day, and that is a real answer.

Things for the Stand: cups $1, table $1, sign $1. Our Time: making it $1, selling it $1. That is $8 of costs, so 2 dollars are left. Set out plain paper and a pencil for each student, and tear 10 scrap-paper squares to show the $10. No drinks are made, bought or sold, and nothing is tasted.

focus: Focus on concrete, visible costs of the lemonade stand (lemons, cups, sign, table)
Simple counting: "How many dollars does the stand pay?"
Visual learning: draw each cost on the board (a lemon, a cup, a sign, a table)
Basic vocabulary: cost, price, need, money, profit
One-step thinking: "What else do we need?"
Add less visible costs (the table, the sign, your time)
Simple categorization: things in the cup, things for the stand, our time
Basic addition: count total number of costs
Introduce "hidden" concept: things you don't see right away
Vocabulary: hidden costs, supplies, time, bulk buying
Include costs you do not see: your time and wasted lemons
Multi-category sorting: direct costs, overhead and labor
Simple calculation: add up estimated costs, compare prices
Understanding your time is a cost even when no one pays you for it
Vocabulary: overhead, waste, labor, bulk buying, true cost
Full cost sheet with direct, overhead and labor totals
Complex calculations: unit price against pack price, and the saving
Understanding the catch in bulk buying (money upfront, wasted extra)
Comparing the first profit guess with profit after all costs
Advanced vocabulary: revenue, expenses, overhead, labor rate, direct costs, bulk buying

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Draw a quick picture beside each cost on the board: a lemon, a cup, a table, a clock for time.
Show cost and profit with the 10 paper clips before writing any words.
Give the frame: "The stand needs ___. That costs $___."

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Start each cost list with one example already filled in.
Let students take away paper clips instead of writing the subtraction.
Let students say their cost list while a partner writes it.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Spread one table cost across ten days of selling and find the cost for one day.
Find a new price for a cup that still leaves a profit after every cost.
Compare a small pack and a big pack of cups and work out the cost of one cup each way.

items: Plain paper — 30 sheets: 10 cut into task cards by the teacher, 20 for the paper airplanes (Tier 1: 10 sheets, task cards only, no paper airplanes)

description.en: Discuss business challenge: when you get too many orders at once. Explain simulation: students will receive multiple task cards at once and must decide what to do first. Review concepts: priority, delegation, time management.
description.es: Discuss business challenge: when you get too many orders at once. Explain simulation: students will receive multiple task cards at once and must decide what to do first. Review concepts: priority, delegation, time management.

sayThis.en: "Sometimes a business gets too many orders at once. Today you get a pile of jobs. You can't do them all. You have to pick what to do first."
sayThis.es: "Sometimes a business gets too many orders at once. Today you get a pile of jobs. You can't do them all. You have to pick what to do first."

watchFor.en: Kids hearing it as a race. Say the goal is picking well, not rushing.
watchFor.es: Kids hearing it as a race. Say the goal is picking well, not rushing.

doneWhen.en: Students can say in their own words what doing first things first means.
doneWhen.es: Students can say in their own words what doing first things first means.

description.en: Talk about a shop that gets too many orders at once. Explain the game: each student gets a pile of job cards at the same time and picks what to do first. Teach three words: first, help and wait.
description.es: Talk about a shop that gets too many orders at once. Explain the game: each student gets a pile of job cards at the same time and picks what to do first. Teach three words: first, help and wait.

sayThis.en: "Sometimes a shop gets too many jobs at once. Today you get a pile of jobs. You can't do them all. You pick which job to do first."
sayThis.es: "Sometimes a shop gets too many jobs at once. Today you get a pile of jobs. You can't do them all. You pick which job to do first."

watchFor.en: Kids hearing it as a race. Say the goal is picking well, not being fast.
watchFor.es: Kids hearing it as a race. Say the goal is picking well, not being fast.

doneWhen.en: Students can say what first, help and wait mean.
doneWhen.es: Students can say what first, help and wait mean.

description.en: Students receive stack of task cards (simple classroom tasks: organize bookshelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers, etc.). Read all tasks. Decide: Which is most urgent? Which takes longest? Which should go first? Make priority list.
description.es: Students receive stack of task cards (simple classroom tasks: organize bookshelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers, etc.). Read all tasks. Decide: Which is most urgent? Which takes longest? Which should go first? Make priority list.

sayThis.en: "Read all your cards. Which job has to be done first? Put it on top. Which one takes the longest? Put it near the bottom."
sayThis.es: "Read all your cards. Which job has to be done first? Put it on top. Which one takes the longest? Put it near the bottom."

watchFor.en: Students starting a job before the pile is sorted. Hold the timer until every pile is in order.
watchFor.es: Students starting a job before the pile is sorted. Hold the timer until every pile is in order.

doneWhen.en: Every student has their cards in a stack or a list in the order they will do them.
doneWhen.es: Every student has their cards in a stack or a list in the order they will do them.

description.en: Students get a pile of job cards (tidy a shelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers and more). The teacher reads the cards out loud. Each student picks the one job to do first and puts that card on top.
description.es: Students get a pile of job cards (tidy a shelf, sharpen pencils, sort papers and more). The teacher reads the cards out loud. Each student picks the one job to do first and puts that card on top.

sayThis.en: "Listen to your job cards. Which job should you do first? Put that card on top."
sayThis.es: "Listen to your job cards. Which job should you do first? Put that card on top."

watchFor.en: Students starting a job before they pick. Hold the timer until every student has a card on top.
watchFor.es: Students starting a job before they pick. Hold the timer until every student has a card on top.

doneWhen.en: Every student has one card picked and on top of the pile.
doneWhen.es: Every student has one card picked and on top of the pile.

description.en: Students work through their tasks in priority order. Set timer. Try to complete as many as possible. If working in pairs, practice delegating: 'You do this one, I'll do that one.' Track what gets done.
description.es: Students work through their tasks in priority order. Set timer. Try to complete as many as possible. If working in pairs, practice delegating: 'You do this one, I'll do that one.' Track what gets done.

sayThis.en: "Timer's on. Start with your top card. Working with a partner? Say, 'You do this one, I'll do that one.'"
sayThis.es: "Timer's on. Start with your top card. Working with a partner? Say, 'You do this one, I'll do that one.'"

watchFor.en: Partners both doing the same card. Point to one card and ask who has it.
watchFor.es: Partners both doing the same card. Point to one card and ask who has it.

doneWhen.en: The timer is done and every student has a done pile and a not-done pile.
doneWhen.es: The timer is done and every student has a done pile and a not-done pile.

description.en: Students do their cards in order. No partners and no splitting jobs. A finished card gets turned face down.

focus: Pick one job card from the pile to do first
Focus on what happens when too many jobs come at once
Teacher-led discussion about when to ask for help
Sort unfinished job cards into do now and can wait
Basic vocabulary: first, too much, help, share, wait
8-10 task cards raced against a timer
Introduction to "first things first" prioritization
Simple delegation: "You do this, I'll do that"
Sort leftover cards into do first, can wait, and skip
Vocabulary expansion: priority, delegate, timer, team, rush
8-10 tasks requiring priority decisions
Use of simple priority matrix (important/urgent)
Team delegation based on skills
Calculate basic earnings and compare scenarios
Vocabulary: prioritize, urgent, important, revenue, wages
Full 8-10 task simulation with solo and team rounds
Detailed priority matrix with all four quadrants
Strategic delegation with role assignment
Financial analysis comparing working alone vs. hiring help
Advanced vocabulary: revenue, wage cost, profit, delegation, priority matrix, hiring plan

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Draw a small picture on each task card (a star, an airplane, blocks) so students can read the job without the words.
Teach busy, help, first and wait with a gesture for each before the solo round.
Give the frame for the team round: "I can do ___. Can you do ___?"

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Give a smaller set of four or five cards in the solo round so the pile does not overwhelm.
Use a clear start and stop signal, like a clap or the lights, not just a spoken word.
Let a student watch the solo round and join in for the team round.

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Record every team's solo and team counts on the board and find which team gained the most.
Work out how many helpers a team could pay before the wages ate all the extra money.
Write a short rule Benny could use to decide when to say "not right now" to a new order.

description.en: Explain 'pivot': when a business changes its product or approach because original plan isn't working. Discuss real examples: a cold-drink stand switches to hot chocolate when it's cold. Introduce challenge scenario.
description.es: Explain 'pivot': when a business changes its product or approach because original plan isn't working. Discuss real examples: a cold-drink stand switches to hot chocolate when it's cold. Introduce challenge scenario.

sayThis.en: "A pivot is when a business changes because the first plan isn't working. A cold-drink stand in the cold can sell hot chocolate instead. That's a pivot."
sayThis.es: "A pivot is when a business changes because the first plan isn't working. A cold-drink stand in the cold can sell hot chocolate instead. That's a pivot."

watchFor.en: Pivot heard as giving up. Say the stand is still open; it just sells something new.
watchFor.es: Pivot heard as giving up. Say the stand is still open; it just sells something new.

doneWhen.en: A student can give one example of a pivot in their own words.
doneWhen.es: A student can give one example of a pivot in their own words.

description.en: Do not use the word pivot. Say change. Draw one example on the board: a cold drink stand in the snow changes to hot chocolate. Draw the before and the after side by side.
description.es: Do not use the word pivot. Say change. Draw one example on the board: a cold drink stand in the snow changes to hot chocolate. Draw the before and the after side by side.

sayThis.en: "Here is a lemonade stand. But look - it is snowing. Nobody wants cold lemonade in the snow. So the stand changes. Now it sells hot chocolate. Same stand, new thing."
sayThis.es: "Here is a lemonade stand. But look - it is snowing. Nobody wants cold lemonade in the snow. So the stand changes. Now it sells hot chocolate. Same stand, new thing."

watchFor.en: Kids thinking the stand closed. Point at the picture and say the stand is still open, it just sells something new.
watchFor.es: Kids thinking the stand closed. Point at the picture and say the stand is still open, it just sells something new.

doneWhen.en: Every student can point to the before picture and the after picture on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every student can point to the before picture and the after picture on the board.

description.en: Students start simple classroom business: selling bookmarks, offering helper services, or making cards. Set up, create product, prepare to sell. Begin initial sales or service.
description.es: Students start simple classroom business: selling bookmarks, offering helper services, or making cards. Set up, create product, prepare to sell. Begin initial sales or service.

sayThis.en: "Make your product — a bookmark, a card, or a helper job. Get it ready. Then start selling to the people near you."
sayThis.es: "Make your product — a bookmark, a card, or a helper job. Get it ready. Then start selling to the people near you."

watchFor.en: Students spending the whole time decorating one item. At four minutes, call "Start selling."
watchFor.es: Students spending the whole time decorating one item. At four minutes, call "Start selling."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a product or service ready and has tried at least one sale.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a product or service ready and has tried at least one sale.

description.en: Everybody makes the same thing: one bookmark. No choosing. When it is made they hold it up and try to sell it to the person beside them.
description.es: Everybody makes the same thing: one bookmark. No choosing. When it is made they hold it up and try to sell it to the person beside them.

sayThis.en: "Everybody makes a bookmark. One bookmark. Color it fast. When it is done, hold it up and try to sell it to the person beside you."
sayThis.es: "Everybody makes a bookmark. One bookmark. Color it fast. When it is done, hold it up and try to sell it to the person beside you."

watchFor.en: Kids coloring one bookmark the whole time. At two minutes say, "Pencils down, start selling."
watchFor.es: Kids coloring one bookmark the whole time. At two minutes say, "Pencils down, start selling."

doneWhen.en: Every student is holding a bookmark.
doneWhen.es: Every student is holding a bookmark.

description.en: Teacher announces a problem: 'No one wants bookmarks today!' or 'We ran out of key materials!' Students must pivot: What could you sell instead with materials you have? What different service could you offer? Quick brainstorm.
description.es: Teacher announces a problem: 'No one wants bookmarks today!' or 'We ran out of key materials!' Students must pivot: What could you sell instead with materials you have? What different service could you offer? Quick brainstorm.

sayThis.en: "Uh-oh. Nobody wants bookmarks today! Look at what's on your desk. What else could you make or do with it?"
sayThis.es: "Uh-oh. Nobody wants bookmarks today! Look at what's on your desk. What else could you make or do with it?"

watchFor.en: Students waiting for new materials. Point to what they already have.
watchFor.es: Students waiting for new materials. Point to what they already have.

doneWhen.en: Every student has named one new idea.
doneWhen.es: Every student has named one new idea.

description.es: The teacher announces one problem: nobody wants bookmarks today. Students look at the paper they already have and name one other thing they could make with it. The teacher gives two examples first.

sayThis.en: "Uh-oh! Nobody wants bookmarks today. Look at your paper. What else could you make? A card? A picture? Tell your partner one."
sayThis.es: "Uh-oh! Nobody wants bookmarks today. Look at your paper. What else could you make? A card? A picture? Tell your partner one."

doneWhen.es: Every student has said one new idea out loud to a partner.

description.es: Students quickly change their business: create new product, switch to different service, or modify original offering. Adapt with available resources. Resume sales or service with new approach.

sayThis.es: "Make the change now. Use only what you have. Then start selling again."

watchFor.es: Tiny changes, like a new colour on the same bookmark. Ask if a customer would want it now.

doneWhen.es: Every student is offering something different from step 2.

description.es: Students change the same paper into the new thing. No new materials. Then hold it up and try to sell it again.

sayThis.es: "Change your paper into the new thing. Use only what you have. Then hold it up and sell it again."

doneWhen.es: Every student is holding up something that is not a bookmark.

description.en: Discuss: Was it hard to pivot? What helped you think of new ideas? Did the pivot work? When should businesses pivot vs. stick with original plan? How do businesses know when to change?
description.es: Discuss: Was it hard to pivot? What helped you think of new ideas? Did the pivot work? When should businesses pivot vs. stick with original plan? How do businesses know when to change?

sayThis.en: "Was it hard to change? Where did your new idea come from? Thumbs up if your pivot worked."
sayThis.es: "Was it hard to change? Where did your new idea come from? Thumbs up if your pivot worked."

watchFor.en: Only the loudest kids answering. Do the thumbs first, then call on a few.
watchFor.es: Only the loudest kids answering. Do the thumbs first, then call on a few.

doneWhen.en: Every student has shown a thumb and at least three have said why.
doneWhen.es: Every student has shown a thumb and at least three have said why.

description.es: Thumbs only. Two questions: was changing hard, and did somebody want your new thing? Skip when a business should change and when it should stay the same.

sayThis.en: "Thumbs up if changing was hard. Now thumbs up if somebody wanted your new thing."
sayThis.es: "Thumbs up if changing was hard. Now thumbs up if somebody wanted your new thing."

watchFor.en: Kids copying the thumb of the child next to them. Have everyone close their eyes for the second question.
watchFor.es: Kids copying the thumb of the child next to them. Have everyone close their eyes for the second question.

doneWhen.en: Every student has shown a thumb for both questions.
doneWhen.es: Every student has shown a thumb for both questions.

discussionQuestions: What did you change about the business?
Would that help? Why?
Is it better to quit or to try something new?

doneWhen.es: Every group is sitting together with a scenario card.

description.es: Groups identify WHY the business is failing. Write or draw the problem.

sayThis.es: "Why is this business in trouble? Write or draw the problem in one sentence."

watchFor.es: Groups jumping straight to fixes. Ask, "What's wrong first?"

watchFor.es: Only one idea, like lower prices. Ask for one change to where or when.

doneWhen.es: Every group has three to five pivots listed.

sayThis.es: "Pick one pivot. Draw a Before side and an After side. Show what changes."

doneWhen.es: Every group has a Before → After chart with one clear change.

description.es: Each group shares their pivot. Class discusses: "Would this work? Why or why not?"

sayThis.es: "Tell us the problem and your pivot. Everyone else, think: would it work? Why or why not?"

description.en: Each team gets a card with four weeks of sales as tally marks, one mark for each thing sold. Count the marks for each product. Draw one bar for each product with crayons on plain paper, one square for each sale. Circle the tallest bar and point to the shortest one.
description.es: Each team gets a card with four weeks of sales as tally marks, one mark for each thing sold. Count the marks for each product. Draw one bar for each product with crayons on plain paper, one square for each sale. Circle the tallest bar and point to the shortest one.

sayThis.en: "Here are your sales. Count the marks. Draw a bar for each thing you sell. Which bar is tallest? Which bar is shortest?"
sayThis.es: "Here are your sales. Count the marks. Draw a bar for each thing you sell. Which bar is tallest? Which bar is shortest?"

watchFor.en: Bars drawn without counting. Count the marks together, then draw one square for each.
watchFor.es: Bars drawn without counting. Count the marks together, then draw one square for each.

doneWhen.en: Every team has a bar for each product and has circled the tallest bar.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a bar for each product and has circled the tallest bar.

sayThis.en: "Four parts. What you're stopping. What you're focusing on. The evidence from your chart. And what it costs you to stop — because stopping something you love is the hard part, and Layla found that out."
sayThis.es: "Four parts. What you're stopping. What you're focusing on. The evidence from your chart. And what it costs you to stop — because stopping something you love is the hard part, and Layla found that out."

doneWhen.en: Every Pivot Plan names one thing being stopped and cites a number from the chart.
doneWhen.es: Every Pivot Plan names one thing being stopped and cites a number from the chart.

watchFor.en: Pivot plans that add something without stopping anything. If nothing stops, nothing changes.
watchFor.es: Pivot plans that add something without stopping anything. If nothing stops, nothing changes.

description.en: Teams complete "Pivot Plan" worksheet: What we're STOPPING (like journals) What we're FOCUSING ON (like pottery) Why this will work (evidence from data) What we'll lose (emotional cost, like Layla missing her journals) What we'll gain (predicted new revenue and profit) Create visual presentation: "Before Pivot" vs. "After Pivot" comparison
description.es: Teams complete "Pivot Plan" worksheet: What we're STOPPING (like journals) What we're FOCUSING ON (like pottery) Why this will work (evidence from data) What we'll lose (emotional cost, like Layla missing her journals) What we'll gain (predicted new revenue and profit) Create visual presentation: "Before Pivot" vs. "After Pivot" comparison

description.en: Teams draw two pictures on plain paper with crayons. The Before picture shows the thing they will stop selling. The After picture shows the thing they will sell more of. Each team says one thing they will miss about the old one.
description.es: Teams draw two pictures on plain paper with crayons. The Before picture shows the thing they will stop selling. The After picture shows the thing they will sell more of. Each team says one thing they will miss about the old one.

sayThis.en: "Draw two pictures. Before: the thing that is not selling. After: the thing you will sell instead. Look at your bars to choose."
sayThis.es: "Draw two pictures. Before: the thing that is not selling. After: the thing you will sell instead. Look at your bars to choose."

watchFor.en: After pictures that show the same thing as Before. Ask, "What did you stop making?"
watchFor.es: After pictures that show the same thing as Before. Ask, "What did you stop making?"

doneWhen.en: Every team has a Before and an After picture, and the After picture matches its tallest bar.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a Before and an After picture, and the After picture matches its tallest bar.

sayThis.en: "Problem, data, decision, prediction. In that order. Investors — your job is to poke holes. Ask why not just drop the price. Ask what if people miss the old thing."
sayThis.es: "Problem, data, decision, prediction. In that order. Investors — your job is to poke holes. Ask why not just drop the price. Ask what if people miss the old thing."

doneWhen.en: Every team has pitched and taken at least two questions.
doneWhen.es: Every team has pitched and taken at least two questions.

watchFor.en: Investors who ask nothing. Give each group one required question off the card.
watchFor.es: Investors who ask nothing. Give each group one required question off the card.

description.en: Each team presents their pivot to "investors" (rest of class) Pitch must include: the problem, the data, the pivot decision, predicted results Investors ask questions: "Why not just lower prices?" "What if people want the old product?" "How do you know this will work?"
description.es: Each team presents their pivot to "investors" (rest of class) Pitch must include: the problem, the data, the pivot decision, predicted results Investors ask questions: "Why not just lower prices?" "What if people want the old product?" "How do you know this will work?"

description.en: Each team shows its Before and After pictures to the class and says three things: what was not selling, what they will sell now, and how their bars show it. Classmates ask one question from the teacher's question card, like "What if people miss the old thing?"
description.es: Each team shows its Before and After pictures to the class and says three things: what was not selling, what they will sell now, and how their bars show it. Classmates ask one question from the teacher's question card, like "What if people miss the old thing?"

sayThis.en: "Show your pictures. Tell us what wasn't selling, what you will sell now, and how your bars show it. Listeners, ask one question."
sayThis.es: "Show your pictures. Tell us what wasn't selling, what you will sell now, and how your bars show it. Listeners, ask one question."

watchFor.en: Teams who only hold up the pictures. Point to each picture and ask them to say that part.
watchFor.es: Teams who only hold up the pictures. Point to each picture and ask them to say that part.

doneWhen.en: Every team has shown its pictures, said all three things, and answered one question.
doneWhen.es: Every team has shown its pictures, said all three things, and answered one question.

sayThis.en: "Here's what happened. Some of these worked and some didn't, and the ones that worked followed the numbers. Layla kept going with what the data said even though she liked the other thing more."
sayThis.es: "Here's what happened. Some of these worked and some didn't, and the ones that worked followed the numbers. Layla kept going with what the data said even though she liked the other thing more."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a post-pivot profit figure written beside its prediction.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a post-pivot profit figure written beside its prediction.

watchFor.en: Teams whose pivot failed taking it personally. Name what their data actually said and where the plan left it.
watchFor.es: Teams whose pivot failed taking it personally. Name what their data actually said and where the plan left it.

description.en: Reveal "results" for each pivot (teacher pre-determines which pivots would succeed based on logic) Calculate new profit numbers Discuss: Which pivots worked best? What made them successful? Connect to Layla's story: "She followed the data even though it was hard. That's what real business owners do."
description.es: Reveal "results" for each pivot (teacher pre-determines which pivots would succeed based on logic) Calculate new profit numbers Discuss: Which pivots worked best? What made them successful? Connect to Layla's story: "She followed the data even though it was hard. That's what real business owners do."

description.en: Tell each team if its sales went up or down after the pivot, using the results you chose before class. Teams show thumbs up or thumbs down. Talk about why some pivots went up. Layla followed her sales even though it was hard.
description.es: Tell each team if its sales went up or down after the pivot, using the results you chose before class. Teams show thumbs up or thumbs down. Talk about why some pivots went up. Layla followed her sales even though it was hard.

sayThis.en: "Here is what happened. Thumbs up if your sales went up. Thumbs down if they went down. The pivots that went up followed the bars."
sayThis.es: "Here is what happened. Thumbs up if your sales went up. Thumbs down if they went down. The pivots that went up followed the bars."

watchFor.en: Teams whose sales went down feeling sad. Show what their bars said and one thing they could try next.
watchFor.es: Teams whose sales went down feeling sad. Show what their bars said and one thing they could try next.

doneWhen.en: Every team knows if its sales went up or down and can say one reason why.
doneWhen.es: Every team knows if its sales went up or down and can say one reason why.

discussionQuestions: What makes a pivot successful vs. a pivot that fails?
How did you use data to make your decision?
Was it hard to stop doing something even if it wasn't working? Why?
When should a business pivot vs. when should it keep trying?
What's the difference between pivoting and quitting?
How do feelings make business decisions harder? (Layla loved journals but had to stop)
extensionIdeas: Track a real local business over a month to see if they change anything
Interview a business owner about times they had to pivot
Create "Pivot or Persist?" decision flowchart
Research famous business pivots (Twitter, Instagram, YouTube)
Calculate: "If Layla kept making journals losing $10/week, how much would she lose in a year?" (opportunity cost)

beforeClass.en: Have the four weeks of sales data printed, or copied by hand onto paper, for every team, and check the numbers actually point somewhere. If the data is ambiguous the pivot becomes a guess. Decide in advance which pivots you'll rule successful in step 5.
beforeClass.es: Have the four weeks of sales data printed, or copied by hand onto paper, for every team, and check the numbers actually point somewhere. If the data is ambiguous the pivot becomes a guess. Decide in advance which pivots you'll rule successful in step 5.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: take pitches from half the teams and have the rest hand in their plans. Short: add a second pivot round after the results are revealed.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: take pitches from half the teams and have the rest hand in their plans. Short: add a second pivot round after the results are revealed.

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Draw a quick before and after picture on the board for each scenario, like an ice cream cone in the snow and then a mug of hot chocolate.
Teach problem, change and pivot with a turning gesture for pivot.
Give the frame: "The problem is ___. We will change ___ to ___."

learningDifferences.label: Students with Learning Differences
strategies: Give a scenario with one clear problem and let the group draw the pivot instead of writing it.
Work in pairs instead of groups of three or four.
Check in during planning with two questions: "What's not working? What could work better?"

advanced.label: Advanced Students
strategies: Work out the business's profit for six weeks after the pivot.
Compare two pivot ideas side by side and explain which one is less risky.
Name a real company that changed what it sells and show its before and after.

description.en: Discuss partnerships: two or more people working together in business. Explain benefits (share work, share ideas) and challenges (must agree, share decisions). Introduce partnership agreement activity.
description.es: Discuss partnerships: two or more people working together in business. Explain benefits (share work, share ideas) and challenges (must agree, share decisions). Introduce partnership agreement activity.

sayThis.en: "A partnership is two people running a business together. You share the work and the ideas. But you have to agree. Today you and a partner will write down how."
sayThis.es: "A partnership is two people running a business together. You share the work and the ideas. But you have to agree. Today you and a partner will write down how."

watchFor.en: Partner heard as best friend. Say partners share a business and have to agree about it.
watchFor.es: Partner heard as best friend. Say partners share a business and have to agree about it.

doneWhen.en: Students can name one good thing and one hard thing about having a partner.
doneWhen.es: Students can name one good thing and one hard thing about having a partner.

description.en: Say partner means two people doing one job together. Show two picture jobs on the board: one draws, one sells. Skip the talk about the hard parts.
description.es: Say partner means two people doing one job together. Show two picture jobs on the board: one draws, one sells. Skip the talk about the hard parts.

sayThis.en: "Today you get a partner. Partners share one business. One person draws. The other person sells. You both get the money."
sayThis.es: "Today you get a partner. Partners share one business. One person draws. The other person sells. You both get the money."

watchFor.en: Partner heard as best friend. Say a partner is the person who shares your job today.
watchFor.es: Partner heard as best friend. Say a partner is the person who shares your job today.

doneWhen.en: Every student can point to the two jobs on the board.
doneWhen.es: Every student can point to the two jobs on the board.

description.en: Students pair up to form business partnerships. Discuss together: What business will we run? What will each partner do? Decide on roles: Who handles money? Who creates product? Who talks to customers? Make initial agreements.
description.es: Students pair up to form business partnerships. Discuss together: What business will we run? What will each partner do? Decide on roles: Who handles money? Who creates product? Who talks to customers? Make initial agreements.

sayThis.en: "Find your partner. What business will you run? Who makes the product? Who talks to customers? Who looks after the money?"
sayThis.es: "Find your partner. What business will you run? Who makes the product? Who talks to customers? Who looks after the money?"

watchFor.en: One partner deciding everything. Ask the quiet partner which job they want.
watchFor.es: One partner deciding everything. Ask the quiet partner which job they want.

doneWhen.en: Every pair has a business idea and a job for each person.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has a business idea and a job for each person.

description.en: The teacher makes the pairs - no choosing partners. Every pair runs the same business, a bookmark stand. Two jobs only: who draws and who sells.

sayThis.en: "Here is your partner. You both run a bookmark stand. One of you draws. One of you sells. Decide who does which."
sayThis.es: "Here is your partner. You both run a bookmark stand. One of you draws. One of you sells. Decide who does which."

doneWhen.en: Every pair has told the teacher who draws and who sells.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has told the teacher who draws and who sells.

description.es: Partners write a simple agreement in pencil on their folded paper: business name, what each person will do (responsibilities), how to make decisions (vote? take turns? discuss?), how to split work fairly. Both partners sign the agreement in pen.

sayThis.en: "Fill in each section on your paper. Business name. Who does what. How you decide. How you split the work. Then you both sign."
sayThis.es: "Fill in each section on your paper. Business name. Who does what. How you decide. How you split the work. Then you both sign."

watchFor.es: Pairs signing before every section is filled. Check the sections before the pens come out.

doneWhen.en: Every pair's paper has all four sections filled and two signatures.
doneWhen.es: Every pair's paper has all four sections filled and two signatures.

watchFor.en: Pairs signing before every section is filled. Check the sections before the crayons come out.

sayThis.en: "Draw you doing your job. Draw your partner doing their job. I will help you write your business name. Then you both sign your name."
sayThis.es: "Draw you doing your job. Draw your partner doing their job. I will help you write your business name. Then you both sign your name."

description.es: Students form pairs based on complementary skills or interests. Partners interview each other: What are your strengths? What do you like doing? What business could we run together? Brainstorm business ideas. Choose one business concept both partners agree on.

sayThis.en: "A partnership is two people agreeing who owns what and who does what. When it goes wrong it's almost never about the work. It's about a thing nobody wrote down at the start."
sayThis.es: "A partnership is two people agreeing who owns what and who does what. When it goes wrong it's almost never about the work. It's about a thing nobody wrote down at the start."

doneWhen.en: At least three things a partnership agreement must cover are listed on the board.
doneWhen.es: At least three things a partnership agreement must cover are listed on the board.

watchFor.en: Partnership heard as just being friends. Say the difference: friends split lunch, partners split money.
watchFor.es: Partnership heard as just being friends. Say the difference: friends split lunch, partners split money.

description.en: Explore business partnerships in depth: legal structures, real partnership agreements, famous successful and failed partnerships. Discuss equity (who owns what percentage), profit sharing, and legal responsibilities. Set ambitious partnership project goals.
description.es: Explore business partnerships in depth: legal structures, real partnership agreements, famous successful and failed partnerships. Discuss equity (who owns what percentage), profit sharing, and legal responsibilities. Set ambitious partnership project goals.

description.en: Talk about partners: two people who run a business together. Talk about sharing jobs and sharing money fairly. Name a few things partners should agree on before they start.
description.es: Talk about partners: two people who run a business together. Talk about sharing jobs and sharing money fairly. Name a few things partners should agree on before they start.

sayThis.en: "Partners run a business together. They agree who does which job. They agree how to share the money. Trouble starts when nobody says it out loud at the start."
sayThis.es: "Partners run a business together. They agree who does which job. They agree how to share the money. Trouble starts when nobody says it out loud at the start."

watchFor.en: Partner heard as just being friends. Say the difference: friends play together, partners run a business together.
watchFor.es: Partner heard as just being friends. Say the difference: friends play together, partners run a business together.

doneWhen.en: At least three things partners should agree on are on the board.

sayThis.en: "Fill in what you're good at and what you want to build. Then find someone whose list is different from yours. Two people who are good at the same thing leave half the business undone."
sayThis.es: "Fill in what you're good at and what you want to build. Then find someone whose list is different from yours. Two people who are good at the same thing leave half the business undone."

doneWhen.en: Every student has a partner and both have completed skills inventories on the table.
doneWhen.es: Every student has a partner and both have completed skills inventories on the table.

watchFor.en: Everyone pairing with their best friend. Say it out loud: pick for the skills, and check the fit by talking first.
watchFor.es: Everyone pairing with their best friend. Say it out loud: pick for the skills, and check the fit by talking first.

description.en: Students answer the skills inventory and business interest survey in pencil on a sheet of paper. Use results to find strategically compatible partners: matching skills to business needs. Partners conduct formal business discussion: visions for business, commitment level, long-term goals. Negotiate and form partnerships based on strategic fit.

description.en: The teacher reads each skills question aloud. Students answer by drawing on their paper with crayons or by telling a partner. Then each student finds a partner who is good at something different.

sayThis.en: "Listen to each question. Draw your answer or tell a friend. What are you good at? What do you like to make? Now find a partner who is good at something different from you."
sayThis.es: "Listen to each question. Draw your answer or tell a friend. What are you good at? What do you like to make? Now find a partner who is good at something different from you."

watchFor.es: Everyone pairing with their best friend. Ask: what is your partner good at that you are not?

doneWhen.es: Every student has a partner and a drawing or an answer about what they are good at.

sayThis.en: "Five answers, together. What you sell. Who buys it. How you make it. What it costs. How you make money. Then draw it as squares and arrows so you can see where the money goes."

description.es: Partners collaboratively develop detailed business model: What will we sell/provide? Who are customers? How will we produce it? What are costs? How will we make profit? Create business model diagram on one sheet of paper showing all components and how they connect.

description.es: Partners use crayons to draw what they will sell and who will buy it, on one sheet of paper.

sayThis.es: "Draw what you will sell. Draw who will buy it. Draw an arrow from your thing to your buyer."

doneWhen.es: Every pair has a drawing of what they sell and who buys it.

sayThis.es: "Now the real thing. Who owns what percentage. What each of you put in. Who does which jobs. Who decides when you disagree. And the awkward one — what happens if one of you wants out."

doneWhen.es: Every agreement has all the required sections filled, including the exit clause.

watchFor.es: Fifty-fifty written everywhere without discussion. Ask if the contributions were actually equal.

description.es: Partners write a detailed partnership agreement on a new sheet of paper covering: ownership percentage, capital contributions (what each brings to business), specific role definitions, daily responsibilities, decision-making protocols, conflict resolution process, financial arrangements, performance expectations, exit strategies.

description.en: Partners draw who does which job on a new sheet of paper. They pick one way to share the money: half each, take turns, or more for more work.
description.es: Partners draw who does which job on a new sheet of paper. They pick one way to share the money: half each, take turns, or more for more work.

sayThis.en: "Draw who does which job. Now pick how you share the money. Half each? Take turns? More for the one who does more work?"
sayThis.es: "Draw who does which job. Now pick how you share the money. Half each? Take turns? More for the one who does more work?"

watchFor.en: Pairs picking half each without talking. Ask if both partners do the same amount of work.
watchFor.es: Pairs picking half each without talking. Ask if both partners do the same amount of work.

doneWhen.en: Every pair has a job drawing and one way to share the money circled.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has a job drawing and one way to share the money circled.

sayThis.en: "Swap with another pair. Read it like you're about to sign it. Is anything unclear? Is one person doing more? What happens when they argue?"
sayThis.es: "Swap with another pair. Read it like you're about to sign it. Is anything unclear? Is one person doing more? What happens when they argue?"

doneWhen.en: Every agreement carries written feedback from another pair.
doneWhen.es: Every agreement carries written feedback from another pair.

watchFor.en: Reviews that just say it's fine. Require one written question per reviewer.
watchFor.es: Reviews that just say it's fine. Require one written question per reviewer.

description.es: Partners exchange agreements with another pair for peer review. Check: Is everything clear? Are responsibilities balanced? Is conflict resolution specified? Provide feedback. Revise agreements based on input.

description.en: Pairs swap agreements with another pair. They check: Does each partner have a job? Does it look fair? They say one thing they like and ask one question. Pairs fix their drawing if they need to.
description.es: Pairs swap agreements with another pair. They check: Does each partner have a job? Does it look fair? They say one thing they like and ask one question. Pairs fix their drawing if they need to.

sayThis.en: "Swap with another pair. Look at their drawing. Does each partner have a job? Does it look fair? Tell them one thing you like and ask one question."
sayThis.es: "Swap with another pair. Look at their drawing. Does each partner have a job? Does it look fair? Tell them one thing you like and ask one question."

watchFor.en: Pairs who only say it looks good. Ask each reviewer for one question out loud.
watchFor.es: Pairs who only say it looks good. Ask each reviewer for one question out loud.

doneWhen.en: Every pair has heard one thing a classmate liked and one question about their agreement.
doneWhen.es: Every pair has heard one thing a classmate liked and one question about their agreement.

sayThis.en: "Make your changes and sign it in pen. Both of you. Then tell me — what was the hardest part to agree on? That's usually the part that matters most."
sayThis.es: "Make your changes and sign it in pen. Both of you. Then tell me — what was the hardest part to agree on? That's usually the part that matters most."

doneWhen.en: Every agreement is signed by both partners with at least one visible revision.
doneWhen.es: Every agreement is signed by both partners with at least one visible revision.

watchFor.en: Signing without making the revisions. Check for a change before the pens come out.
watchFor.es: Signing without making the revisions. Check for a change before the pens come out.

description.en: Partners finalize and sign their partnership agreements. Discuss: What surprised you about creating an agreement? What might be hard in real partnerships? Why do written agreements matter? How does your partnership agreement protect both partners?
description.es: Partners finalize and sign their partnership agreements. Discuss: What surprised you about creating an agreement? What might be hard in real partnerships? Why do written agreements matter? How does your partnership agreement protect both partners?

sayThis.en: "Make your changes and sign it in crayon. Both of you. Then tell me — what was the hardest part to agree on? That's usually the part that matters most."
sayThis.es: "Make your changes and sign it in crayon. Both of you. Then tell me — what was the hardest part to agree on? That's usually the part that matters most."

watchFor.en: Signing without making the revisions. Check for a change before the crayons come out.

discussionQuestions: What negotiation strategies worked best for reaching agreement?
Did any partnership split money unevenly? Why was that fair?
What's the difference between a fair split and an equal split?
Why do real businesses write contracts instead of just making promises?
What clause in your agreement do you think will be most important?
In the story, what would have happened if Ellen and the friends DIDN'T write everything down?
extensionIdeas: Compare to real-world business partnerships (research famous business partnerships)

Research consignment vs. other partnership types (joint venture, LLC, etc.)

ell.label: English Language Learners
strategies: Draw a simple picture beside each agreement heading on the board, like a name tag for Business Name and two hands for Who Does What.

strategies: Give a folded agreement with the headings already written and blanks to fill in.

description.en: Students become store owners. Teacher announces: 'It's almost winter holiday!' Students must predict demand and 'buy' inventory. description.en: You're a store manager before the holidays. Show product cards with varying demand levels. Introduce the problem: you must order products NOW for customers who will shop LATER. Order too much = waste money. Order too little = miss sales.
description.es: You're a store manager before the holidays. Show product cards with varying demand levels. Introduce the problem: you must order products NOW for customers who will shop LATER. Order too much = waste money. Order too little = miss sales.

sayThis.en: "You run a store before the holidays. You order now, but customers shop later. Order too much and you waste money. Order too little and customers leave with nothing."
sayThis.es: "You run a store before the holidays. You order now, but customers shop later. Order too much and you waste money. Order too little and customers leave with nothing."

watchFor.en: The idea that ordering lots is always safe. Ask what happens to the things nobody buys.
watchFor.es: The idea that ordering lots is always safe. Ask what happens to the things nobody buys.

doneWhen.en: Students can name one risk of ordering too much and one of ordering too little.
doneWhen.es: Students can name one risk of ordering too much and one of ordering too little.

description.en: Students review last year's sales data (simplified cards) and make ordering decisions for 5-6 products. Write predictions in pencil on the team's paper: how many of each item will sell this holiday season?
description.es: Students review last year's sales data (simplified cards) and make ordering decisions for 5-6 products. Write predictions in pencil on the team's paper: how many of each item will sell this holiday season?

sayThis.en: "Look at last year's sales on the board. For each product, write how many you think will sell this year. Every item you order comes out of your $200."
sayThis.es: "Look at last year's sales on the board. For each product, write how many you think will sell this year. Every item you order comes out of your $200."

watchFor.en: Last year's numbers copied exactly. Ask if anything might be different this year.
watchFor.es: Last year's numbers copied exactly. Ask if anything might be different this year.

doneWhen.en: Every team has a number for every product and a budget card with the cost taken off.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a number for every product and a budget card with the cost taken off.

description.en: Teams look at last year's sales on the board for two products. For each one they choose: more, less or the same as last year. They write or draw how many of each they will order.
description.es: Teams look at last year's sales on the board for two products. For each one they choose: more, less or the same as last year. They write or draw how many of each they will order.

sayThis.en: "Look at last year's sales on the board. Will more people buy this year, fewer, or the same? Pick one for each product. Each thing you order costs $1 of your $10."
sayThis.es: "Look at last year's sales on the board. Will more people buy this year, fewer, or the same? Pick one for each product. Each thing you order costs $1 of your $10."

watchFor.es: Teams picking the same as last year every time. Ask if anything might be different this year.

doneWhen.en: Every team has a number for both products and a budget card with the dollars crossed off.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a number for both products and a budget card with the dollars crossed off.

description.en: Reveal actual demand (draw customer cards). Students check if they had enough inventory. Calculate: items sold, items left over (wasted money), customers turned away (lost sales).
description.es: Reveal actual demand (draw customer cards). Students check if they had enough inventory. Calculate: items sold, items left over (wasted money), customers turned away (lost sales).

sayThis.en: "Now I draw the customer cards. For each product, did you have enough? Count what you sold, what's left, and how many customers you turned away."
sayThis.es: "Now I draw the customer cards. For each product, did you have enough? Count what you sold, what's left, and how many customers you turned away."

watchFor.en: Teams selling more than they ordered. You can't sell what isn't on the shelf.
watchFor.es: Teams selling more than they ordered. You can't sell what isn't on the shelf.

doneWhen.en: Every team has sold, left over and turned away written for each product.
doneWhen.es: Every team has sold, left over and turned away written for each product.

description.en: Calculate profit: revenue from sales minus cost of all inventory ordered (including unsold items). Compare results across the class. Who was the best store manager? What strategy did they use?
description.es: Calculate profit: revenue from sales minus cost of all inventory ordered (including unsold items). Compare results across the class. Who was the best store manager? What strategy did they use?

sayThis.en: "Money from sales, take away what you paid for everything you ordered — even the things that didn't sell. Who made the most? What did they do?"
sayThis.es: "Money from sales, take away what you paid for everything you ordered — even the things that didn't sell. Who made the most? What did they do?"

watchFor.en: Unsold items left out of the cost. Ask, "Did you pay for those?"
watchFor.es: Unsold items left out of the cost. Ask, "Did you pay for those?"

doneWhen.en: Every team has a profit number and the class has named the best manager's strategy.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a profit number and the class has named the best manager's strategy.

description.en: Teams count the items they sold and the items left over, and say which number is bigger instead of working out profit. The class names the team with the fewest left over and what they did.
description.es: Teams count the items they sold and the items left over, and say which number is bigger instead of working out profit. The class names the team with the fewest left over and what they did.

sayThis.en: "How many did you sell? How many are left? Which number is bigger? Which team had the fewest left over? What did they do?"
sayThis.es: "How many did you sell? How many are left? Which number is bigger? Which team had the fewest left over? What did they do?"

watchFor.en: Teams counting leftovers as sold. Ask: did a customer buy this one?
watchFor.es: Teams counting leftovers as sold. Ask: did a customer buy this one?

doneWhen.en: Every team has said sold and left over, and the class has named what the best team did.
doneWhen.es: Every team has said sold and left over, and the class has named what the best team did.

description.en: Why is predicting hard? What clues help stores prepare? (Weather, trends, past data.) How do real stores handle leftover holiday inventory? (Sales, clearance, donations.)
description.es: Why is predicting hard? What clues help stores prepare? (Weather, trends, past data.) How do real stores handle leftover holiday inventory? (Sales, clearance, donations.)

sayThis.en: "Why is guessing hard? What clues help — weather, trends, last year? And what do stores do with leftovers?"
sayThis.es: "Why is guessing hard? What clues help — weather, trends, last year? And what do stores do with leftovers?"

watchFor.en: Answers like just guess better. Ask what they would look at first.
watchFor.es: Answers like just guess better. Ask what they would look at first.

doneWhen.en: The board lists at least three clues and two things stores do with leftovers.
doneWhen.es: The board lists at least three clues and two things stores do with leftovers.

discussionQuestions: Which product was hardest to predict? Why?
Did anyone run out of inventory? How did that feel?
Did anyone make too many and have leftovers? What's the cost of that?

How could you use last year's data to predict this year better?

beforeClass.en: Write five or six product cards and a customer card with the real demand for each. Put last year's sales on the board. Make each team a $200 budget card on scrap paper, and decide the order cost and the selling price for each product.
beforeClass.es: Write five or six product cards and a customer card with the real demand for each. Put last year's sales on the board. Make each team a $200 budget card on scrap paper, and decide the order cost and the selling price for each product.

runningLongOrShort.en: Long: in step 4, compare only the top two teams instead of the whole class. Short: after step 5, draw new customer cards for a second season and let teams reorder.
runningLongOrShort.es: Long: in step 4, compare only the top two teams instead of the whole class. Short: after step 5, draw new customer cards for a second season and let teams reorder.

beforeClass.en: Write two product cards on scrap paper, bookmarks and pencils, and a customer card with the real demand for each. Put last year's sales for those two products on the board. Make each team a $10 budget card on scrap paper. Each item costs $1 to order.

sayThis.en: "You run a shop for a year. Three seasons, and you order stock before you know what sells. Order too little and you lose sales. Order too much and it sits there costing you. Nobody gets this perfectly right."
sayThis.es: "You run a shop for a year. Three seasons, and you order stock before you know what sells. Order too little and you lose sales. Order too much and it sits there costing you. Nobody gets this perfectly right."

doneWhen.en: The three seasons and last year's chart are up where everyone can read them.
doneWhen.es: The three seasons and last year's chart are up where everyone can read them.

description.es: Introduce the retail challenge: managing a store through three seasons (back-to-school, holiday, summer). Each season has different demand patterns. Show historical sales data charts.

sayThis.en: "Look at last September before you order anything. What do children need in the first week of school? Write your order and commit to it."
sayThis.es: "Look at last September before you order anything. What do children need in the first week of school? Write your order and commit to it."

doneWhen.en: Every team has a written, committed order for all products.
doneWhen.es: Every team has a written, committed order for all products.

watchFor.es: Orders written without looking at the historical chart. Send them back to it once.

description.es: Review last year's back-to-school data. Teams decide how much of each product to order and write it in pencil on their paper. Consider: What do students need in September? How much should you stock?

sayThis.es: "Here's what actually sold. Work out your profit or your loss. Then say out loud what you'd change — that sentence is your strategy for the next round."

doneWhen.es: Every team has a profit or loss figure and a written change for next round.

watchFor.en: Blame on bad luck. Point at the historical chart they had in front of them.
watchFor.es: Blame on bad luck. Point at the historical chart they had in front of them.
